tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

A workflow size guideline is configured for this session: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale.

Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. For a biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature question, the firecrawl_research_* tools search the paper index, while categories: ["research"] on firecrawl_search filters ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites. Use the firecrawl_research_* tools to search academic and research literature, expand from anchor papers via the citation graph, and read full-text passages from a specific paper. Search and discovery tools … [truncated]

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.
- Keep one working tab per task/site. Before opening another, inspect
  `current_tab()` and `list_tabs()` and use `switch_tab()` to reuse a matching
  tab. Do not le… [truncated]

Read-only access to the user's Zotero research library. For substantive sport-science questions, build a Zotero-first evidence pack before answering. Return bounded page-located evidence, label external fallback sources explicitly, and never represent a Reference Stub as a reviewed Paper Brief. SecondBrain Queue is the priority lane; promotion eligibility is controlled by promotion_scope.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_scrape
entries.description:
Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state.

`firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call.

Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

toolDetail.description: URL mode only: domain discovery detail, summary by default; compact returns provider/capability/description, full includes contracts. Ignored with alexandria.

domainTools.description: URL mode only: include domain-matched Alexandria tools for the page in tools on the returned document. Ignored with alexandria.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_search
entries.description:
Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`.

For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`.

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts.

Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Use ["alexandria"] alone for provider discovery without web results.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation. `developer` returns hits in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`; the other categories also filter `data.web`.

# AGENTS.md

Project: Flint

## What this is
Flint is Claude working as Eric's sport-science, performance, S&C and rehab thought
partner. This repo builds the knowledge base behind that role. It catalogs Eric's
Drive (his own material, TB's Training Info, Landon Evans, courses, papers), routes the
high-value sources into Zotero and the SecondBrain vault, and writes per-discipline
synthesis notes that compare the sources against Eric's own method. It is a side-lane
project, outside the prioritization-slate cap. See `README.md` for the approach and
`docs/PLAN.md` for the checklist.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- `data/` is gitignored except aggregate summaries. Regenerate the file-level manifest with `pwsh scripts/build_manifest.ps1`.
- Codex workers read staged copies in `staging/`, never the Drive root. DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult and PFF exports are never catalogued.
- The ingest review gate has two stages.

  2. Before promoting, Codex reviews the staged entries against the staged sources, with instructions to falsify (`staging/review_<source>_codex.md`). Nothing reaches the vault without a GO or a GO AFTER FIXES that has been applied.
- Library entries label every voice. The source author's statements are plain. Eric's judgments get "Eric's review:". The entry writer's own reasoning gets "Inference:". No unlabeled judgments. ## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

# Atomization brief (shared by every Flint ingest agent)

Read this whole file before writing anything. It holds the rules the Harries review taught (2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes). The review gate will check every rule here.

## Schema

Follow `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\ingest-book\SKILL.md` exactly: `_domain.md`, `_book.md` (map and resume checkpoint, updated after EACH chapter or unit), and entries named `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md` with kind one of principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim. Use the frontmatter keys exactly as the skill gives them. The body has **What it is** / **Why it works** / **When to apply** / **When NOT to apply** (mandatory, non-trivial) / **Example** / **Related**.

Style reference, read before writing: `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library\strength-and-conditioning\fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer\case-study--isometric-sprinter-and-hurdler.md`, plus one principle file in the same folder.

## Voices: label every one

- **The source author's statements are plain text.**
- **Eric's views** (from `docs/method-baseline.md` or his reviews) are prefixed "Eric's baseline:" or "Eric's review:".
- **Your own reasoning, application or synthesis** is prefixed "Inference:".
- **Nothing unlabeled that the author did not say.** The most common failures: a judgment from Eric's review written as if the author said it; a mechanism the author never gave presented as "why it works" (write "The author gives no mechanism. Inference: ..."); an invented example.

## Lessons from the Supertraining Chapter 1 review (2026-09-26: 30 FIX, 1 NO-GO of 41)

- **Keep the source's internal contradictions.** When a book says X on one page and not-X on another, record both with their pages and set `contested`. Never pick one side silently. The NO-GO entry reversed the book's SJ-CMJ strength-deficit rule because the book states it both ways.
- **Name the right voice.** In co-authored books, write "the authors" unless a passage clearly belongs to one author. A passage that names Verkhoshansky in the third person is Siff writing.
- **Keep `proven` rare and scoped.** Scope it to the replicated core (for example, "Hill's force-velocity curve"), never the whole entry, and mark any disputed sentence inside it. Four of eight `proven` ratings were lowered.
- **No mechanism the source does not give.** About a dozen "Why it works" sections supplied physiology the book never states. Label it "Inference:" or leave it out.
- **Do not add "well established" or "modern research shows" without a citation.** Name the paper, or delete the phrase.

## Evidence

- Every number, definition and quote carries a checkable locator: PDF page (and printed page if it differs), or file plus timestamp. Never write "confirmed in PDF" unless you opened that page.
- Never invent a number. Keep ambiguity visible: mark unclear audio or OCR as unclear, and do not harmonize two conflicting numbers from the source; record both with their locators.
- OCR sources (`staging/ocr/*.md`): pages listed as low_confidence in the header must be checked against the page image before any number from them is cited. Use the Read tool on the PDF page, or render it.

## Confidence

- Practitioner courses and lectures: ceiling `supported`.
- Books: `proven` only for established, widely replicated physiology or mechanics. Soviet-era or single-lab empirical findings and training prescriptions: `supported` at most. `untested` for single cases and anecdotes. `contested` where another library source or modern evidence disagrees (say which).

## Dedup and converge

Before each entry, grep `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library` and the staging library (`C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\staging\library`) for the concept. If it is covered, add a new entry only for a genuinely new angle, and link the existing one in Related. List reciprocal-link suggestions in your final report. Never edit files in the vault or another agent's staging folder.

## Baylor context

Read `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\docs\method-baseline.md` (approved). Use it in When to apply, labelled "Eric's baseline:". Department names: Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine, Applied Performance. Plain style, no em dashes. Use commas, colons and parentheses.

## Scope and output

- Write ONLY into your assigned staging folder. No git, no vault edits.
- Stop at a chapter or unit boundary. It is better to finish fewer chapters well; the `_book.md` checkpoint lets the next batch resume.
- Final reply: entries by kind and by confidence; chapters or units done and pending with page ranges; reciprocal-link suggestions; unclear or contradictory spots in the source; anything you could not read.

entries.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

+**What it is** — The authors state spinal ligament involvement during deadlifting or
+cleans is valuable for reducing the stress placed on the erector spinae, and that spinal
+flexion during heavy lifts from the ground can damage intervertebral discs; a competent
+lifter actively increases erector spinae tension to diminish flattening of the lumbar spine
+during the lift. If this active tension is overdone, the spinal ligaments become slack and
+most of the load is instead borne by the muscles; conversely, if the muscles are
+inadequately contracted, excessive stress is placed on the ligaments. The authors describe
+a skilled lifter as one able to optimize the balance between spinal muscles and ligaments,
+enhancing lifting efficiency and reducing injury likelihood; they state similar rhythms and
+patterns of muscular and other soft-tissue involvement are essential for strength-training
+efficiency and safety generally. (PDF p. 209, printed pp. 198-199.)
+**Why it works** — The authors give no cited source or measured data for this specific
+muscle-ligament load-sharing claim in this passage; it follows logically from the joint
+stabilization sequence described elsewhere in the chapter (muscle/SEC as primary
+stabilizer, ligament/PEC engaging as muscular contribution changes; see
+[[framework--joint-stabilization-sequence-across-range-of-motion]]), applied here
+specifically to the lumbar spine during a pull, but is not derived from a named study.
+**When to apply** — Useful as a coaching frame for cueing lumbar position during heavy
+deadlifts and cleans: the goal is neither maximal erector spinae tension (which the text
+says can make ligaments too slack to share load appropriately) nor minimal tension
+(overloading the ligaments and discs), but an actively maintained, non-flexed lumbar
+position that keeps both tissues sharing the load as intended.
+**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence `untested`: no citation or measured data given for
+this specific claim in this passage.** Do not present this as an established biomechanical
+finding to Athletic Medicine or in athlete-facing injury-risk communication without
+independent verification; it is the authors' own technique-coaching synthesis. This entry
+is about muscle-ligament load *sharing*, distinct from the moment-arm/torque-reduction
+principle already in this library (see
+[[principle--torque-optimization-in-lifting-technique]]), which addresses keeping the bar
+path close to the body rather than the muscle-versus-ligament balance at the lumbar spine
+itself.
+**Example** — Inference: a lifter who rounds the lower back on a heavy deadlift (excess
+lumbar flexion, per this claim, meaning inadequately contracted erector spinae) shifts more
+stress onto the spinal ligaments and discs than a lifter who maintains a neutral,
+actively-braced lumbar spine throughout the pull.

+[[principle--torque-optimization-in-lifting-technique]].

+alone. The text states directly that "enhanced strength is of little value if the athlete
+does not maintain or improve neuromuscular ability" (printed 134), and that reaction time
+"comprises a sensing time and a decision time, with the latter in particular improving
+through the regular application of neuromuscular skill training" (printed 134); "movement
+time is strongly influenced by motor coordination or precision of movement" (printed 135).
+Elsewhere in the same section (printed 140), the text states that "quickness is a general
+quality of the CNS ... determined by genetic factors, and therefore the potential for its
+development is limited," while separately, "speed of movement ... [has] far greater
+potential to enhance" than quickness does; this entry records both the latency-is-fixed
+finding here and that later statement rather than picking one. (PDF pp. 144-146, printed
+pp. 133-135, "Quickness and Reactive Ability"; PDF p. 151, printed p. 140.)
**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is that latency reflects largely fixed
-neural-transmission and central-processing constraints (peripheral sensory-to-CNS and
-CNS-to-muscle conduction delays plus a genetically-set neuronal firing-rate threshold),
-while movement time (coordination, precision, motor-unit recruitment efficiency once the
-decision/signal has fired) is the part of the chain that skill practice and strength/rate-of-force-development
-training can actually shorten.
+neural-transmission and central-processing constraints: peripheral sensory-to-CNS and
+CNS-to-muscle conduction delays. Hanes and Schall (1996), cited for the firing-rate finding,
+concern variability in how a monkey's neuronal firing rate reaches a fixed
+movement-triggering threshold, not a claim that the threshold itself is genetically set; that
+broader genetic claim is the text's own separate statement about the latency period, not
+something Hanes and Schall themselves establish. Movement time, per the text, "is strongly
+influenced by motor coordination or precision of movement" (printed 135) rather than by
+strength or rate-of-force-development training specifically; **Inference:** to the extent
+strength/RFD training changes movement time, the text does not say so directly.
**When to apply** — Use this distinction when interpreting or designing "reaction" drills:
a drill meant to improve true reaction time (auditory/visual go-signal to first movement)

"""Mechanical pre-promotion lint for Flint staged library folders.

Usage: python lint_library.py <book-folder> [<book-folder> ...]
Checks: body em dashes (header separators allowed), unresolved [[links]] (against staging
library + vault), review-history narration, confidence values, required sections.
"""
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

STAGING = Path(r"C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\staging\library")
VAULT = Path(r"C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library")
HEADER = re.compile(r"^\*\*[^*]+\*\* —")
HISTORY = re.compile(r"prior version|earlier draft|NO-GO|round[- ]1|round[- ]2|fix pass|fixer|this revision|previous version", re.I)
CONF = {"proven", "supported", "untested", "contested"}
SECTIONS = ["**What it is**", "**When NOT to apply**"]

known = set()
for root in (STAGING, VAULT):
    for p in root.rglob("*.md"):
        known.add(p.stem)
        known.add(p.relative_to(root).with_suffix("").as_posix())
        known.add(p.parent.name + "/" + p.stem)

problems = 0
for folder in sys.argv[1:]:
    for f in sorted(Path(folder).glob("*.md")):
        text = f.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        issues = []
        body_dash = [i + 1 for i, line in enumerate(text.splitlines())
                     if "—" in HEADER.sub("", line)]
        if body_dash:
            issues.append(f"body em dash lines {body_dash[:8]}")
        for link in re.findall(r"\[\[([^\]|#]+)", text):
            link = link.strip().removesuffix(".md")
            if link not in known and link.split("/")[-1] not in known:
                issues.append(f"unresolved [[{link}]]")
        if not f.name.startswith("_"):
            m = re.search(r"^confidence:\s*(\S+)", text, re.M)
            if not m or m.group(1).strip("\"'") not in CONF:
                issues.append(f"confidence={m.group(1) if m else 'missing'}")
            for s in SECTIONS:
                if s not in text:
                    issues.append(f"missing {s}")
            h = HISTORY.findall(text)
            if h:
                issues.append(f"review-history words {sorted(set(x.lower() for x in h))}")
        if issues:
            problems += len(issues)
            print(f"{f.parent.name}/{f.name}: " + "; ".join(issues))
print(f"TOTAL ISSUES: {problems}")

# SecondBrain Vault — Conventions

Writing-and-synthesis vault. Plain markdown, no plugin dependencies. See
`README.md` for the folder philosophy and pilot history.

## Folder semantics (who writes where)

| Folder | Contains | Written by |
|--------|----------|-----------|
| `Inbox/` | Raw capture: interview transcripts, synced meetings, weekly reviews. Cooling-off zone — nothing lives here permanently. | `interview-me`, `meeting-sync`, `weekly-review`, graphify |
| `Notes/` | Atomic permanent notes, one idea per file. | `interview-me` (0–3 per day, only when earned) |
| `Knowledge/` | Evergreen reference. Two kinds: **ingested** external resources (articles, books, frameworks) and **harvested** lesson articles from shipped work. Sub-segmented — see below. | `ingest-resource`, `ingest-book`, `/harvest` |
| `Projects/` | Fuel for active work — research, assets, graphify output, project meetings. | `ingest-resource`, graphify, `meeting-sync` |
| `output/` | `_ledger.md` — running record of shipped artifacts. | `/harvest`, by hand |
| `Drafts/` | Essays/talks-in-progress assembled from linked Notes. | by hand |
| `Archive/` | Published/shipped writing, out of active surface. | by hand |

## Knowledge sub-segmentation

`Knowledge/` root should stay empty — every note lands in a subfolder. Segmented
2026-07-27 because 44 loose files spanned two unrelated domains, so a work query
swept 29 sermon notes it could never use.

| Subfolder | Contains |
|---|---|
| `faith/` | Sermons, church gatherings, biblical study, spiritual formation |
| `sport-science/` | Training methodology, GPS/force-plate references, injury frameworks, cited papers |
| `career-strategy/` | Career positioning, research strategy, interview debriefs |
| `library/` | Advisor book library (`ingest-book`) |
| `frameworks/`, `coaching-frameworks/` | Named frameworks kept as standalone reference |

Routing rule is unchanged — **shelf life decides `Knowledge/` vs `Projects/`**;
these subfolders only decide *where inside* `Knowledge/`. Add a subfolder rather
than dropping a file at the root.

## Archive

`Archive/interviews/` holds daily interview transcripts older than ~30 days.
`Inbox/` says nothing lives there permanently, so transcripts move here once
their content has been distilled into `Notes/`. Wikilinks still resolve —
Obsidian matches `[[2026-06-04-interview]]` by filename regardless of folder.

## The harvest rule

Evergreen **lesson articles** in `Knowledge/` are written ONLY after something
ships — harvested from finished projects via `/harvest`, never speculatively.
(Ingesting *external* reference material via `ingest-resource`/`ingest-book`
is exempt: that's filing someone else's evergreen content, not writing your own.)

## File conventions

- **Filenames:** kebab-case slug of the title (`adoption-is-the-bottleneck.md`).
- **Never overwrite** an existing note. Slug collision → append `-2` or ask to merge.
- **Frontmatter** on every generated note: `type` (resource | harvest | note |
  ledger), `created` (YYYY-MM-DD), `source`, `domain: []`, `tags: []`, `status`.
- **Wikilinks:** link the first mention of any concept/person/project that has
  an existing note. Related-but-unmentioned notes go in a `## Related` section
  (2–5 links max). Links to not-yet-existing notes are allowed sparingly for
  concepts worth a future note.
- **Route by shelf life, not topic:** still true in a year → `Knowledge/`;
  fuel for current work → `Projects/`. Raw capture only ever enters via `Inbox/`.

## Git

The vault is backed up to GitHub (`erash11/SecondBrain`). Commits are backup
artifacts, not reviewed code — commit generated/updated notes with a short
message; don't leave vault changes uncommitted at the end of a session.

"""Promote reviewed book folders from staging/library into the SecondBrain vault.

    python scripts/promote_to_vault.py <domain>/<book> [...]            # dry run
    python scripts/promote_to_vault.py <domain>/<book> [...] --apply    # copy

Dry run reports, per book: files new to the vault, files that differ, files only in the
vault (never deleted), and every [[link]] in the promoted files that would not resolve
against the vault as it will be after promotion. _domain.md files are never copied over an
existing vault file (merge those by hand); a domain new to the vault gets its staged
_domain.md. Nothing is committed: commit in the vault afterwards.
"""
import argparse
import filecmp
import re
import shutil
import sys
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
STAGING = ROOT / "staging" / "library"
VAULT = Path(r"C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library")
LINK = re.compile(r"\[\[([^\]|#\n]+)")


def names(p: Path, root: Path) -> set[str]:
    rel = p.relative_to(root).with_suffix("").as_posix()
    return {p.stem, rel, f"{p.parent.name}/{p.stem}"}


def main() -> int:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("books", nargs="+", help="<domain>/<book> under staging/library")
    ap.add_argument("--apply", action="store_true")
    a = ap.parse_args()

    known: set[str] = set()
    for p in VAULT.rglob("*.md"):
        known |= names(p, VAULT)
    plan = []
    for book in a.books:
        src = STAGING / book
        if not src.is_dir():
            print(f"missing staging folder: {src}")
            return 2
        for p in src.glob("*.md"):
            known |= names(p, STAGING)
        plan.append((book, src, VAULT / book))

    unresolved = 0
    for book, src, dst in plan:
        new = [p.name for p in src.glob("*.md") if not (dst / p.name).exists()]
        changed = [p.name for p in src.glob("*.md")
                   if (dst / p.name).exists() and not filecmp.cmp(p, dst / p.name, shallow=False)]
        vault_only = sorted(p.name for p in dst.glob("*.md") if not (src / p.name).exists()) if dst.exists() else []
        print(f"\n== {book}: {len(new)} new, {len(changed)} changed, {len(vault_only)} vault-only")
        for n in changed:
            print(f"   changed: {n}")
        for n in vault_only:
            print(f"   VAULT-ONLY (kept, check for a rename): {n}")
        for p in src.glob("*.md"):
            for link in LINK.findall(p.read_text(encoding="utf-8")):
                link = link.strip().removesuffix(".md")
                if link not in known and link.split("/")[-1] not in known:
                    unresolved += 1
                    print(f"   UNRESOLVED in {p.name}: [[{link}]]")
        domain = src.parent / "_domain.md"
        if not (dst.parent / "_domain.md").exists() and domain.exists():
            print(f"   new domain: will copy {domain.parent.name}/_domain.md")
        if a.apply:
            dst.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
            for p in src.glob("*.md"):
                shutil.copy2(p, dst / p.name)
            if not (dst.parent / "_domain.md").exists() and domain.exists():
                shutil.copy2(domain, dst.parent / "_domain.md")
    print(f"\nunresolved links: {unresolved}; {'APPLIED' if a.apply else 'dry run, nothing written'}")
    return 1 if unresolved else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

Library entries: the text is added as a new line at the end of the **Related** paragraph, or
a **Related** paragraph is created at the end of the file. Paper briefs: added as a bullet
under "## Related knowledge" (replacing a "None identified" placeholder). A row is skipped
when the source already links the target.
"""
import argparse
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

VAULT = Path(r"C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library")


def resolve(src: str) -> Path | None:
    src = src.strip().strip("`")

def add(text: str, line: str) -> str:
    lines = text.rstrip("\n").split("\n")
    if "## Related knowledge" in text:
        i = next(k for k, l in enumerate(lines) if l.startswith("## Related knowledge"))
        j = i + 1
        while j < len(lines) and not lines[j].startswith("## "):
            j += 1
        block = [l for l in lines[i + 1:j] if l.strip() and "None identified" not in l]
        return "\n".join(lines[:i + 1] + [""] + block + [f"- {line}", ""] + lines[j:]).rstrip("\n") + "\n"
    rel = [k for k, l in enumerate(lines) if l.startswith("**Related**")]
    if rel:
        j = rel[-1] + 1
        while j < len(lines) and lines[j].strip() and not lines[j].startswith("**"):
            j += 1
        return "\n".join(lines[:j] + [line] + lines[j:]) + "\n"
    return "\n".join(lines + ["", f"**Related** — {line}"]) + "\n"

        path = resolve(src)

            continue
        body = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        if re.search(r"\[\[[^\]]*" + re.escape(slug) + r"[\]|#]", body):

            continue

            path.write_text(add(body, text), encoding="utf-8")
    print(f"\n{done} {'added' if a.apply else 'to add'}, {skipped} already linked, {failed} unresolved")
    return 1 if failed else 0

"""Append reciprocal Related links from a staging/reciprocal_links_*.md table to vault files.

    python scripts/apply_reciprocal_links.py staging/reciprocal_links_2026-09-27.md           # dry run
    python scripts/apply_reciprocal_links.py staging/reciprocal_links_2026-09-27.md --apply

Run AFTER promote_to_vault.py --apply, so every source file is in the vault. Table rows:
| source (path under Knowledge/library, domain optional) | [[target]] | location | text | origin |
Library entries: the text is added as a new line at the end of the **Related** paragraph, or
a **Related** paragraph is created at the end of the file. Paper briefs: added as a bullet
under "## Related knowledge" (replacing a "None identified" placeholder). A row is skipped
when the source already links the target.
"""
import argparse
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

VAULT = Path(r"C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library")


def resolve(src: str) -> Path | None:
    src = src.strip().strip("`")
    hits = [p for p in VAULT.rglob("*.md") if p.as_posix().endswith("/" + src)]
    return hits[0] if len(hits) == 1 else None


def add(text: str, line: str) -> str:
    lines = text.rstrip("\n").split("\n")
    if "## Related knowledge" in text:
        i = next(k for k, l in enumerate(lines) if l.startswith("## Related knowledge"))
        j = i + 1
        while j < len(lines) and not lines[j].startswith("## "):
            j += 1
        block = [l for l in lines[i + 1:j] if l.strip() and "None identified" not in l]
        return "\n".join(lines[:i + 1] + [""] + block + [f"- {line}", ""] + lines[j:]).rstrip("\n") + "\n"
    rel = [k for k, l in enumerate(lines) if l.startswith("**Related**")]
    if rel:
        j = rel[-1] + 1
        while j < len(lines) and lines[j].strip() and not lines[j].startswith("**"):
            j += 1
        return "\n".join(lines[:j] + [line] + lines[j:]) + "\n"
    return "\n".join(lines + ["", f"**Related** — {line}"]) + "\n"


def main() -> int:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("table")
    ap.add_argument("--apply", action="store_true")
    a = ap.parse_args()
    rows = [r for r in Path(a.table).read_text(encoding="utf-8").split("\n## Dropped")[0].splitlines()
            if r.startswith("| ") and "[[" in r]
    done = skipped = failed = 0
    for r in rows:
        cells = [c.strip() for c in r.strip().strip("|").split("|")]
        src, target, text = cells[0], cells[1], cells[3]
        slug = re.search(r"\[\[([^\]|]+)", target).group(1).split("/")[-1]
        path = resolve(src)
        if path is None:
            failed += 1
            print(f"UNRESOLVED source: {src}")
            continue
        body = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        if re.search(r"\[\[[^\]]*" + re.escape(slug) + r"[\]|#]", body):
            skipped += 1
            continue
        done += 1
        print(f"{'ADD' if a.apply else 'would add'}: {path.relative_to(VAULT).as_posix()} -> {slug}")
        if a.apply:
            path.write_text(add(body, text), encoding="utf-8")
    print(f"\n{done} {'added' if a.apply else 'to add'}, {skipped} already linked, {failed} unresolved")
    return 1 if failed else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

"""Copy promoted book folders (and their domains' _domain.md) from the vault back into staging.

    python scripts/sync_back_from_vault.py <domain>/<book> [...]

Run after promotion and after reciprocal links are applied in the vault, so staging matches
the canonical vault copy and a later promote dry run shows 0 changed for these books.
"""
import shutil
import sys
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
STAGING = ROOT / "staging" / "library"
VAULT = Path(r"C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library")

domains = set()
for book in sys.argv[1:]:
    src, dst = VAULT / book, STAGING / book
    n = 0
    for p in src.glob("*.md"):
        shutil.copy2(p, dst / p.name)
        n += 1
    domains.add(book.split("/")[0])
    print(f"{book}: {n} files synced")

# AGENTS.md

Project: Flint

## What this is
Flint is Claude working as Eric's sport-science, performance, S&C and rehab thought
partner. This repo builds the knowledge base behind that role. It catalogs Eric's
Drive (his own material, TB's Training Info, Landon Evans, courses, papers), routes the
high-value sources into Zotero and the SecondBrain vault, and writes per-discipline
synthesis notes that compare the sources against Eric's own method. It is a side-lane
project, outside the prioritization-slate cap. See `README.md` for the approach and
`docs/PLAN.md` for the checklist.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- `data/` is gitignored except aggregate summaries. Regenerate the file-level manifest with `pwsh scripts/build_manifest.ps1`.
- Codex workers read staged copies in `staging/`, never the Drive root. DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult and PFF exports are never catalogued.
- The ingest review gate has two stages.
  1. Before atomizing, verify the source artifact by an independent route: page order, scanned versus text, transcripts checked against captions.
  2. Before promoting, Codex reviews the staged entries against the staged sources, with instructions to falsify (`staging/review_<source>_codex.md`). Nothing reaches the vault without a GO or a GO AFTER FIXES that has been applied.
- Library entries label every voice. The source author's statements are plain. Eric's judgments get "Eric's review:". The entry writer's own reasoning gets "Inference:". No unlabeled judgments. Every number carries a timestamp or page the reviewer can check, and a claim is only tagged "confirmed in PDF" if that PDF is staged. (Learned from the Harries review, 2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes, mostly for attribution.)
- Writing: plain, direct, no em dashes. Documents use the Baylor design system.

# Issurin 2016 — Benefits and limitations of block-periodized preparation

> **Citation**
> Issurin, V. B. (2016). Benefits and limitations of block periodized training approaches to athletes' preparation: A review. *Sports Medicine, 46*(3), 329–338. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-015-0425-5

## Why it was promoted

This review distinguishes concentrated-unidirectional and multi-targeted block models and provides a useful conceptual vocabulary for discussing concentrated workloads and sequencing.

## Research question

What benefits, limitations, and sport-context boundaries are reported for two versions of block-periodized athlete preparation?

## Population and context

- The review emphasizes elite, subelite, and well-trained athletes across endurance, team, combat, dual, jumping, and strength/power settings. [p. 11]
- It also discusses a smaller number of recreational-athlete studies.
- It is a training-theory review, not evidence specific to collegiate American football.

## Study design and methods

- Narrative review contrasting concentrated-unidirectional and multi-targeted block-periodization models.
- The article summarizes prior studies in tables but does not report a systematic search, eligibility process, formal risk-of-bias appraisal, or meta-analysis.
- Consequently, the stated number and direction of supportive studies should be interpreted as an author-curated synthesis rather than a pooled comparative estimate.

## Key findings

- Concentrated-unidirectional programs in combat and team sports improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team practice or competitive performance. [p. 6]
- In an elite-swimmer example, specific strength and anaerobic capacity improved but swimming performance improved in only two of three athletes. [p. 6]
- The author judged the concentrated-unidirectional evidence insufficient for broad implementation in high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation. [p. 6]
- The review reports support from 28 studies for multi-targeted block programs, but the designs, populations, outcomes, and comparator quality varied. [p. 11]
- The concentrated-unidirectional model was presented as better suited to sports dominated by a narrow target quality and as restricted when peak performance requires many interacting abilities. [p. 11]

## Limitations and applicability

- Non-systematic study selection and absent risk-of-bias assessment create a substantial risk of selective emphasis.
- Fitness improvements are not interchangeable with sport-specific performance, availability, or competitive outcomes. [p. 6]
- Training models were not consistently isolated from total volume, intensity, exercise choice, coaching, or athlete history.
- Evidence spans dissimilar sports and training levels; it does not supply validated block durations or effect estimates for collegiate American football.
- The strong conclusion favoring multi-targeted block periodization is the author's synthesis and should not be treated as settled comparative evidence. [p. 11]

## Practitioner interpretation

Use block periodization as a planning hypothesis: concentrate compatible emphases when competition structure and athlete needs justify it, while maintaining the qualities and technical exposure that cannot safely decay. Judge the plan by sport-specific performance, availability, and individual response—not by the periodization label. Compare it prospectively with the program's own prior practice where feasible.

## Evidence map

| Claim | Locator | Evidence type |
|---|---|---|
| Review scope and distinction between two models | p. 4 | narrative framing |
| Concentrated-unidirectional evidence and performance gaps | p. 6 | narrative synthesis |
| Multi-targeted evidence claim and applicability boundaries | p. 11 | narrative synthesis/limitation |

## Related knowledge

- [[periodization]] — annual and phase planning
- [[training-load-concentration]] — sequencing compatible emphases

# Synthesis note template

One note per practical question, drafted in `docs/synthesis/`, reviewed by Eric, then promoted to
the vault and linked from the domain advisor. A note is finished when Eric has answered its open
questions, not when it is written. Length: 2 to 3 pages.

## Voices (same rules as the library)
- Source claims are plain text with a `[[library-entry]]` link and the entry's confidence in brackets, e.g. `[supported]`.
- Evidence from Zotero or the web that is not a library entry is labelled **External:** with author, year and page.
- Eric's documented positions (`docs/method-baseline.md`) are labelled **Eric's baseline:**. Positions from the HHPR 5355 transcripts are labelled **Course baseline (HHPR 5355, speaker unconfirmed):** until Eric claims them.
- The writer's own synthesis is labelled **Inference:**.
- No em dashes. Plain, direct sentences.

## Sections
1. **The question**: as asked, and how it actually breaks down. Say plainly when the sources answer a different question from the one being asked.
2. **Bottom line**: 3 to 5 sentences a coach could act on, each tagged with its confidence.
3. **Where the sources agree**: each point with links and confidence.
4. **Where they disagree**: both sides, links, confidence, and what would settle it.
5. **What transfers and what does not**: when the sources come from a different sport or population.
6. **What none of them covers**: gaps, and which uningested chapter or paper would fill each.
7. **Eric's baseline**: the documented positions, labelled as above, and how they sit against sections 3 to 5.
8. **Questions for Eric**: 4 to 6 numbered questions whose answers would settle the note.
9. **Sources used**: library entries (with confidence) and external papers.

  1. **Ronnestad 2011** (EXTERNAL; also summarized in Zotero BVP63L4A, PDF p. 6): one strength session per week kept the preseason strength and 40-m sprint gains over 12 in-season weeks. This only fits one planned peak, such as the gap before a title game or bowl, not every week.
  3. **Wellman 2019** (Zotero 396EV93N, PDF p. 6): in one NCAA D-I program, every preseason week carried more load than every in-season week. The staff cut practice length on Tuesday and Wednesday in weeks 9-12 while keeping the intensity days. That is a season-scale taper already done by cutting duration.
  4. **Issurin 2008** (EXTERNAL, table read from the author's PDF): max speed is retained for about 5 ± 3 days, and strength and aerobic qualities for about 30 ± 5 days. Saldanha 2026 (EXTERNAL) supports the short speed figure: after a 5-day in-season break, soccer players lost max velocity and repeated-sprint ability while strength and jump held.     - Marrier 2017 was checked against its abstract only.

Against that: Bompa's 3:1 rule (supported, Ch 1) and Verkhoshansky's Banister model and taper studies (supported, PDF pp. 99-100). Evans objects to one model covering every quality at once, and Verkhoshansky says the model must be fitted to each athlete, so they are closer than they look.
  - D-3: Issurin 2008 against Issurin 2016 on lower-level athletes. The book says medium concentration is enough for them (contested, PDF p. 44). The review says amateurs face "no serious restrictions" with concentrated blocks (paper brief, p. 11). The review's critique of concentrated single-quality blocks is aimed at Verkhoshansky's model, not the book's.
  - D-4: How hard to cut a taper. Issurin says a short taper needs a fast decrease (supported, PDF p. 123). Fitz-Clarke 1991 says tapers "may be too rigorous and short" (supported, printed 88-89).
  - D-5: Heavy lifting in the taper. Platonov & Fesenko say reduce it; Bompa & Carrera say keep sport-specific strength. Both appear in the same Issurin entry (supported, PDF p. 108). This is the "lift heavy in bowl week" question.
  - D-6: How long qualities last after training stops. Issurin Table 1.6 (contested, PDF p. 35) says aerobic lasts longest and speed shortest. Eric's own course material (class-4-2026.md p. 47) says aerobic is lost fastest and speed slowest. The entry says not to reconcile them; this needs Eric's call.
  - D-7: In-season emphasis. Issurin prioritizes max strength; Newton 2006 sequences heavy lifting with ballistic work. Both are in the same entry (supported, PDF pp. 109-110).
  - D-8: Monitoring during the hardest training block. The book's retelling of Hooper says subjective ratings were enough. The entry's check of the original abstract found n = 14, some circularity, and catecholamines adding prediction (supported, PDF p. 121). Eric's baseline adds that the department's daily wellness survey was gamed at roster scale.
  - D-9: Evidence for periodization at all. Evans's "classic literature supports it" (untested, U3 L4) against Afonso 2019 (no study tested whether peaks land when predicted) and Harries 2015 (linear and undulating give equal strength gains).
  
  **Gaps no entry answers from a source (where only the entry writer's inference exists, I counted it as a gap)**
  1. Bye weeks.
  2. Short weeks and Thursday or Friday games.
  3. The move from fall camp to week 1.
  4. Postseason and the bowl gap. The bowl-prep structures are all inference from kayak and pre-Olympic calendars, and nothing covers a conference championship followed by an uncertain bowl date.
  5. Position-group differences in taper or maintenance dose.
  6. Any taper dose-response study in football.
  7. Detraining across a football season. The only figure is Fleck & Kraemer, secondhand.
  8. What to give low-snap and non-playing players in season.
  9. Travel, the academic calendar and NCAA practice-hour limits.
  10. Kickoff time of day.
  11. How long sports form lasts once reached. Bondarchuk only gives the time to enter it.
  
  Uningested sources that would help:
  - Bompa Ch 7 "Peaking for Competition", plus Ch 5, 6 and 8
  - Issurin Ch 4-5
  - Verkhoshansky Ch 4-9
  - Bondarchuk Ch 3
  - Fullagar 2017 (full text; currently a stub)
  
  **Two things worth passing to Eric**
  1. Two Issurin entries attribute a sentence to "Issurin's own later peer-reviewed review": that block-periodization evidence "does not supply validated block durations... for collegiate American football." The entries are framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks and framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring. In the Issurin 2016 paper brief, that sentence is an unlocated Limitations bullet written by the brief writer. Under the voice rules it should be relabeled as an inference in both entries.
  2. Research-paper briefs have no `confidence:` field, and the Bompa Ch 1-2 entries give only chapter locators. The synthesis cannot rank those against book entries or check Bompa claims page by page.

- WT\docs\synthesis\_work\peaking-external-evidence.md: Zotero and external papers, labelled.
- WT\docs\method-baseline.md lines 84-88 and 143-150 and tension 9 (line ~195). No em dashes. Plain, direct sentences; Eric wants tangible, usable guidance, so the Bottom line must be concrete (e.g. weekly max-velocity exposure, one heavy strength session per week floor) with confidence tags.

Write to WT\docs\synthesis\peaking-and-taper-in-season-football.md with frontmatter: type: synthesis, discipline: strength-and-conditioning, question, status: draft (awaiting Eric's review), created: 2026-09-27, sources: [list of books/papers]. -# When a Training Stage Outruns the 30-Day Residual Clock, Insert a Mini-Block, Don't Just Add Workouts
-**What it is** — This section directly answers the mismatch already flagged in
-[[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]: the accumulation
-mesocycle's basic-ability residual runs out at about **30 days** (Table 1.6; see
-[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]), which caps how long the
-following transmutation-plus-realization stretch can run before basic abilities decay below
-target. But Issurin notes many sports need their transmutation mesocycle to run **3-4 weeks**
-for anaerobic glycolytic development, and the realization mesocycle (taper) can run **about two
-weeks**: together, roughly **five weeks**, which already exceeds the ~30-day strength-aerobic
-residual (PDF pp. 129-130, printed pp. 118-119; verified against page image). Issurin's stated
-fix: do **not** simply add extra aerobic or strength workouts into the transmutation mesocycle
-to "top up" the decaying residual. This fails because the highly intense transmutation
-mesocycle actively suppresses the immediate effect of aerobic training, and the anabolic
-strength stimulus needs recovery time the transmutation mesocycle cannot spare. Instead, insert
-a **special compact mini-block (a short microcycle)** dedicated to the decaying ability. Figure
-3.12 (PDF p. 130, printed p. 119; re-verified against the page image, 2026-09-27) diagrams the
-resulting pattern for a training stage, in sequence: **accumulation** (high-volume basic
-aerobic-strength workloads, **20-25 days**), then **transmutation** (highly intensive specific
-workloads, **20-25 days**), then **realization** (taper and maximal speed, **10-16 days**), then
-**competition**. The figure's "Mini-block inclusion" callout points to more than one insertion,
-not a single one: an accumulation-type (aerobic-strength) patch sits inside the transmutation
-span, a transmutation-type (highly intensive specific) patch sits inside the realization span,
-and a second accumulation-type patch also sits inside the realization span: three mini-block
-insertions total across the diagram, not one. Issurin gives a worked contrast of two
-real scheduling situations (PDF p. 131, printed p. 120): when two targeted competitions are set
-**a five-week interval** apart (his cited example: kayaking's European and World Championships,
-which happen to fall five to six weeks apart in a typical calendar),
-the fix is to compress the whole stage (10-14 days accumulation, 10-14 days transmutation, 8-10
-days realization), short enough that the accumulation mesocycle's own residual still covers the
-whole stage, so **no mini-block is needed at all**. When circumstances instead force a longer,
-**7-9 week** training stage (his example: pre-Olympic preparation, where the international
-calendar has no tune-up competitions before the Games), the recommended answer is to plan longer
-mesocycles **and** include the mini-block, because a stage that long cannot otherwise carry the
-accumulation-phase residual all the way to competition. **Inference:** the chapter's own summary
-restates the placement rule concretely: an **aerobic mini-block can be inserted inside the
-transmutation mesocycle**, and a **highly intense anaerobic mini-block can be inserted inside
-the realization mesocycle** (PDF p. 132, printed p. 121); reading this alongside Figure 3.12's
-three patches, each mesocycle gets a short dose of whichever ability it does not otherwise
-train, timed to arrive before that ability's own residual clock runs out (this synthesis
-across the figure and the summary sentence is the writer's own connection, not stated by
-Issurin in one place).
-**Why it works** — The author gives a reason why *added workouts* fail, but hedges the
-proposed remedy rather than explaining why it succeeds. His stated reason additional workouts
-fail, scoped to the transmutation mesocycle specifically: the transmutation mesocycle
-"strongly suppresses the immediate effect of aerobic training," and added strength work
-"require[s] sufficient recovery that cannot be provided" inside a mesocycle built for a
-different, fatiguing purpose (PDF p. 130, printed p. 119). For the remedy itself, Issurin
-writes only: "**Apparently**, what should be inserted in the mesocycle is not several
-additional workouts but a special compact mini-block (short microcycle), in order to prolong
-training residuals" (PDF p. 130, printed p. 119), his own hedge word, not a stated mechanism
-for why a discrete mini-block succeeds where added workouts fail. No outcome data for the
-mini-block approach is presented in this section; Figure 3.12 cites Issurin & Lustig (2004), a
-coaching-practice article in *Leistungssport*, not a controlled study. **Inference:** a
-plausible reason a discrete mini-block might succeed is that it is short enough to insert
-without abandoning the surrounding mesocycle's main purpose while still being its own coherent
-loading-then-recovery unit rather than scattered single sessions, but this is the writer's own
-extrapolation, not something Issurin states.
-**When to apply: this is the entry most directly responsive to the strength-and-conditioning
-miss-log's "peaking phase structure for collegiate football" gap (logged 2026-09-03), and the
-clearest football calendar mapping in this chapter, Inference throughout** —
-- **The gap between the final regular-season or conference-championship game and a bowl game**
-  (commonly roughly 3-6 weeks depending on bowl selection and game date) is structurally the
-  same scheduling decision Issurin poses in his worked example. A **short** gap (roughly
-  5-6 weeks or less) should be handled like his compressed-stage case: run a short
-  accumulation-transmutation-realization sequence sized to fit inside the gap (e.g., 10-14 days
-  rebuild / 10-14 days sharpen / remaining days as realization/taper), in which case a
-  strength-aerobic residual built at the very start plausibly survives to the bowl game without
-  needing a mini-block. A **longer** gap (closer to 6+ weeks, which happens for some
-  earlier-selected bowls) more closely resembles his 7-9 week pre-Olympic case: plan a longer
-  rebuild phase **and** insert an aerobic (or strength) mini-block partway through the
-  bowl-prep transmutation-equivalent work, specifically to protect the basic conditioning base
-  built early in the gap from decaying below target by game day.
-- **In-season, week to week:** [[case-study--popov-competition-shortens-residual-effects]]
-  already shows that a hard game can itself accelerate residual decay; a bye week, or a week
-  after an unusually taxing game, is a natural, calendar-given opportunity to run something like
-  Issurin's aerobic mini-block (a few days of concentrated aerobic-strength work) to "top up" a
-  basic-ability residual before it drops further, rather than treating every week's training
-  content as identical regardless of how the prior weeks' games affected the athletes.
-- **Eric's baseline** does not currently name a mini-block concept or an explicit bowl-prep
-  periodization structure at all. **Inference:** this is the writer's own assessment, not
-  Eric's: among the Chapter 3 entries produced so far, this framework reads as the single most
-  direct, numerically specific answer this ingest has produced to that gap, and should be
-  flagged to Eric as a candidate structure to react to, not an already-adopted practice.
-**When NOT to apply** — **Population caveat, repeated deliberately because this is
-the chapter's central prescriptive claim:** every piece of evidence behind this framework
-(the 30-day residual table, the kayaking/pre-Olympic worked examples, the Popov case) comes from
-individual, endurance-or-technical Olympic sports with a fixed, known international competition
-calendar set months or years in advance. Football's bowl-selection process is itself uncertain
-until late in the season (a team does not always know its exact bowl date and opponent far in
-advance), which makes pre-planning an exact-length rebuild-then-taper sequence harder than in
-Issurin's kayaking example, where the championship dates are fixed well ahead of the season.
-**Inference:** none of Issurin's specific day-counts (20-25 / 20-25 / 10-16 days; the 5-6 week
-vs. 7-9 week contrast) were derived from or tested against a team-contact-sport calendar; they
-should be treated as a structural template to adapt to football's specific bowl-selection
-timeline and roster fatigue state at season's end (which is itself compounded by an already-long
-season, unlike Issurin's examples where the "prior mesocycle" is a dedicated, undisturbed
-accumulation block rather than 12+ weeks of in-season competition). The mini-block's own
-duration is not specified numerically in this section (Issurin calls it a "short microcycle,"
-consistent with the 2-4 day aerobic contrast mini-block already given in
-[[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]'s Table 3.10):
-treat 2-4 days as the applicable figure by cross-reference, not as independently stated here.
-Issurin gives his own explicit limit on this whole residual-clock logic, immediately before
-this section: "if the training design is based solely on the length of training residuals, it
-will be extremely rigid and inflexible. There are also other factors influencing training
-residuals" (PDF p. 127, printed p. 116); the training stage itself he defines as three
-consecutive mesocycle-blocks "vary[ing] from 4-10 weeks" (same locator). This entry's
-day-count-driven Example below should be read against that caveat, not as a rigid formula.
-Issurin's own later peer-reviewed review states that block-periodization evidence "does not
-supply validated block durations or effect estimates for collegiate American football"
-(Issurin, 2016, *Sports Medicine*, vault
-`research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a.md`).
-**Example** — **Inference:** for a **4-week gap** between a team's last game and its bowl game,
-Issurin's own worked 5-week case (10-14 / 10-14 / 8-10 days) states plainly that "you need not
-include mini-blocks because the training residuals following the accumulation mesocycle
