+# When a Training Stage Outruns the 30-Day Residual Clock, Insert a Mini-Block, Don't Just Add Workouts
+**What it is** — This section directly answers the mismatch already flagged in
+[[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]: the accumulation
+mesocycle's basic-ability residual runs out at about **30 days** (Table 1.6; see
+[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]), which caps how long the
+following transmutation-plus-realization stretch can run before basic abilities decay below
+target. But Issurin notes many sports need their transmutation mesocycle to run **3-4 weeks**
+for anaerobic glycolytic development, and the realization mesocycle (taper) can run **about two
+weeks**: together, roughly **five weeks**, which already exceeds the ~30-day strength-aerobic
+residual (PDF pp. 129-130, printed pp. 118-119; verified against page image). Issurin's stated
+fix: do **not** simply add extra aerobic or strength workouts into the transmutation mesocycle
+to "top up" the decaying residual. This fails because the highly intense transmutation
+mesocycle actively suppresses the immediate effect of aerobic training, and the anabolic
+strength stimulus needs recovery time the transmutation mesocycle cannot spare. Instead, insert
+a **special compact mini-block (a short microcycle)** dedicated to the decaying ability. Figure
+3.12 (PDF p. 130, printed p. 119; re-verified against the page image, 2026-09-27) diagrams the
+resulting pattern for a training stage, in sequence: **accumulation** (high-volume basic
+aerobic-strength workloads, **20-25 days**), then **transmutation** (highly intensive specific
+workloads, **20-25 days**), then **realization** (taper and maximal speed, **10-16 days**), then
+**competition**. The figure's "Mini-block inclusion" callout points to more than one insertion,
+not a single one: an accumulation-type (aerobic-strength) patch sits inside the transmutation
+span, a transmutation-type (highly intensive specific) patch sits inside the realization span,
+and a second accumulation-type patch also sits inside the realization span: three mini-block
+insertions total across the diagram, not one. Issurin gives a worked contrast of two
+real scheduling situations (PDF p. 131, printed p. 120): when two targeted competitions are set
+**a five-week interval** apart (his cited example: kayaking's European and World Championships,
+which happen to fall five to six weeks apart in a typical calendar),
+the fix is to compress the whole stage (10-14 days accumulation, 10-14 days transmutation, 8-10
+days realization), short enough that the accumulation mesocycle's own residual still covers the
+whole stage, so **no mini-block is needed at all**. When circumstances instead force a longer,
+**7-9 week** training stage (his example: pre-Olympic preparation, where the international
+calendar has no tune-up competitions before the Games), the recommended answer is to plan longer
+mesocycles **and** include the mini-block, because a stage that long cannot otherwise carry the
+accumulation-phase residual all the way to competition. **Inference:** the chapter's own summary
+restates the placement rule concretely: an **aerobic mini-block can be inserted inside the
+transmutation mesocycle**, and a **highly intense anaerobic mini-block can be inserted inside
+the realization mesocycle** (PDF p. 132, printed p. 121); reading this alongside Figure 3.12's
+three patches, each mesocycle gets a short dose of whichever ability it does not otherwise
+train, timed to arrive before that ability's own residual clock runs out (this synthesis
+across the figure and the summary sentence is the writer's own connection, not stated by
+Issurin in one place).
+**Why it works** — The author gives a reason why *added workouts* fail, but hedges the
+proposed remedy rather than explaining why it succeeds. His stated reason additional workouts
+fail, scoped to the transmutation mesocycle specifically: the transmutation mesocycle
+"strongly suppresses the immediate effect of aerobic training," and added strength work
+"require[s] sufficient recovery that cannot be provided" inside a mesocycle built for a
+different, fatiguing purpose (PDF p. 130, printed p. 119). For the remedy itself, Issurin
+writes only: "**Apparently**, what should be inserted in the mesocycle is not several
+additional workouts but a special compact mini-block (short microcycle), in order to prolong
+training residuals" (PDF p. 130, printed p. 119), his own hedge word, not a stated mechanism
+for why a discrete mini-block succeeds where added workouts fail. No outcome data for the
+mini-block approach is presented in this section; Figure 3.12 cites Issurin & Lustig (2004), a
+coaching-practice article in *Leistungssport*, not a controlled study. **Inference:** a
+plausible reason a discrete mini-block might succeed is that it is short enough to insert
+without abandoning the surrounding mesocycle's main purpose while still being its own coherent
+loading-then-recovery unit rather than scattered single sessions, but this is the writer's own
+extrapolation, not something Issurin states.
+**When to apply: this is the entry most directly responsive to the strength-and-conditioning
+miss-log's "peaking phase structure for collegiate football" gap (logged 2026-09-03), and the
+clearest football calendar mapping in this chapter, Inference throughout** —
+- **The gap between the final regular-season or conference-championship game and a bowl game**
+  (commonly roughly 3-6 weeks depending on bowl selection and game date) is structurally the
+  same scheduling decision Issurin poses in his worked example. A **short** gap (roughly
+  5-6 weeks or less) should be handled like his compressed-stage case: run a short
+  accumulation-transmutation-realization sequence sized to fit inside the gap (e.g., 10-14 days
+  rebuild / 10-14 days sharpen / remaining days as realization/taper), in which case a
+  strength-aerobic residual built at the very start plausibly survives to the bowl game without
+  needing a mini-block. A **longer** gap (closer to 6+ weeks, which happens for some
+  earlier-selected bowls) more closely resembles his 7-9 week pre-Olympic case: plan a longer
+  rebuild phase **and** insert an aerobic (or strength) mini-block partway through the
+  bowl-prep transmutation-equivalent work, specifically to protect the basic conditioning base
+  built early in the gap from decaying below target by game day.
+- **In-season, week to week:** [[case-study--popov-competition-shortens-residual-effects]]
+  already shows that a hard game can itself accelerate residual decay; a bye week, or a week
+  after an unusually taxing game, is a natural, calendar-given opportunity to run something like
+  Issurin's aerobic mini-block (a few days of concentrated aerobic-strength work) to "top up" a
+  basic-ability residual before it drops further, rather than treating every week's training
+  content as identical regardless of how the prior weeks' games affected the athletes.
+- **Eric's baseline** does not currently name a mini-block concept or an explicit bowl-prep
+  periodization structure at all. **Inference:** this is the writer's own assessment, not
+  Eric's: among the Chapter 3 entries produced so far, this framework reads as the single most
+  direct, numerically specific answer this ingest has produced to that gap, and should be
+  flagged to Eric as a candidate structure to react to, not an already-adopted practice.
+**When NOT to apply** — **Population caveat, repeated deliberately because this is
+the chapter's central prescriptive claim:** every piece of evidence behind this framework

+individual, endurance-or-technical Olympic sports with a fixed, known international competition

+Issurin's kayaking example, where the championship dates are fixed well ahead of the season.

+vs. 7-9 week contrast) were derived from or tested against a team-contact-sport calendar; they
+should be treated as a structural template to adapt to football's specific bowl-selection
+timeline and roster fatigue state at season's end (which is itself compounded by an already-long
+season, unlike Issurin's examples where the "prior mesocycle" is a dedicated, undisturbed
+accumulation block rather than 12+ weeks of in-season competition). The mini-block's own
+duration is not specified numerically in this section (Issurin calls it a "short microcycle,"
+consistent with the 2-4 day aerobic contrast mini-block already given in
+[[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]'s Table 3.10):
+treat 2-4 days as the applicable figure by cross-reference, not as independently stated here.
+Issurin gives his own explicit limit on this whole residual-clock logic, immediately before
+this section: "if the training design is based solely on the length of training residuals, it
+will be extremely rigid and inflexible. There are also other factors influencing training
+residuals" (PDF p. 127, printed p. 116); the training stage itself he defines as three
+consecutive mesocycle-blocks "vary[ing] from 4-10 weeks" (same locator). This entry's

+phase, since a stage approaching that length is closer to where Issurin says the accumulation
+residual alone cannot cover the whole stage; note that Figure 3.12's own 20-25 / 20-25 / 10-16
+day figures apply to the longer 7-9 week stage, not to a 6-week gap, so they should not be used
+as the target durations here. Per the caveat above, treat both of these as a structural
+template to react to, not a rigid formula: "there are also other factors influencing training

-# Transmutation Mesocycle: Capped at About Four Weeks by Fatigue and by the Aerobic Residual Clock
-**What it is** — The transmutation mesocycle "transmutes accumulated basic abilities into
-specific physical and techno-tactical fitness" and is characterized by more specialized
-targeted abilities, higher-intensity/higher-volume developmental workloads, and being "the most
-fatiguing mesocycle" (PDF p. 118, printed p. 107; verified against page image). Table 3.9 gives
-three duration-limiting factors: **fatigue accumulation** from highly concentrated intense
-workloads approaches its upper limit in **3-4 weeks** (obviated by inserting a restorative
-microcycle or an aerobic mini-block); **the residual training effect of the preceding
-(accumulation) mesocycle**, since after 4 weeks of highly intense work the effect of the prior
-aerobic-strength mesocycle "drops dramatically," per the roughly 30-day residual windows in
-[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]; and **the competition
-calendar**, which can force a shorter mesocycle regardless of the other two factors. Net rule:
-the transmutation mesocycle "usually lasts no more than four weeks" (PDF pp. 118-119, printed
-pp. 107-108). Issurin flags a real methodical contradiction here: many sports need anaerobic
-glycolytic development over a longer period than four weeks allows without letting the
-accumulation mesocycle's aerobic/strength residual decay; the stated fix is inserting a
-short aerobic mini-block inside the transmutation mesocycle (elaborated in
-[[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]]). The book also states a
-season-dependence on which factor binds: early in the season, fatigue accumulation limits
-mesocycle duration; late in the season, the competition calendar does instead (PDF p. 119,
-printed p. 108). (Source quirk, not corrected here: the text's own cross-reference "see 3.3.3"
-at this point, PDF p. 119 / printed p. 108, points to a section that does not exist in this
-book; the actual relevant material is 3.3.2.) Content (Table 3.10, PDF p. 119,
-printed p. 108) sequences: an **initial** loading microcycle (usually one week) with gradually
-increasing load; **mid-and-ending** loading and/or impact microcycles (impact can run 3-4 days);
-and optional insertions, including a **competition/trial** microcycle (participating fatigued is
-not excluded; athletes tend to experience the competitive workload itself as a relative load
-reduction, and expect no personal best from it), a **restoration** microcycle (planned in
-advance or triggered individually as athletes near their adaptation limit), or a short
-**aerobic contrast mini-block** (2-4 days, to prolong aerobic training residuals and partly
-restore athletes for the next high-intensity stretch). Monitoring (Table 3.11, PDF p. 120,
-printed p. 109) again tracks workload performance, targeted (sport-specific) ability results,
-and training responses, but with an added emphasis here: **subjective self-estimation of
-fatigue, stress, sleep, and muscle soreness**, because "maximal workloads elicit maximal
-training responses" and "much confidence between the coach and athlete is very important."
-Because dosing near the "upper limits of adaptation" is described as the transmutation
-mesocycle's biggest problem, Issurin gives Peter Snell's (Olympic champion runner and sport
-physiologist) definition of overtraining: "a state in which performance diminishes while the
-level of training is maintained or increased" (Snell, 1990), and lists five early warning
-signals (Burke et al., 1990; Hooper et al., 1995, PDF p. 121, printed p. 110): resting HR up
-more than **5 beats/min over 3-5 days**; persistent or rapid body-mass decrease; persistent
-increased general fatigue; persistent increased muscle soreness; persistent increased sleep
-disturbance. A supporting case study (Hooper et al., 1995, same locator): **19 elite swimmers**
-monitored over 6 months with a large blood/urine/hormone/CPK/HR/blood-pressure battery plus
-daily self-reported stress, fatigue, sleep quality, and muscle soreness (1-7 scale); **three**
-swimmers were diagnosed overtrained during the study, but stale-vs-non-stale athletes did
-**not** differ on any blood, urine, or physiological marker at mid- or late-season. The
-difference showed up clearly and significantly only in the subjective fatigue/soreness
-ratings, and a multi-component model using those four subjective ratings predicted competitive
-performance changes; adding more objective indicators did not improve prediction accuracy.
-Hooper's effective discriminating tool, per the book's own description, was the 4-item, 1-7
-daily self-rating log (fatigue, stress, sleep, soreness), itself a daily wellness check, not
-a separate instrument from what it is being compared against (PDF p. 121, printed p. 110).
-**Inference, from the primary abstract (Hooper et al., 1995, *Medicine & Science in Sports &
-Exercise* 27:106-112, retrieved via Europe PMC):** the study monitored **14** swimmers, not
-19 as the book states. Staleness was classified partly *from* prolonged, high fatigue-rating
-levels, which makes a fatigue-rating prediction of staleness partly circular by construction.
-Late-season stress ratings plus resting plasma catecholamines explained 85% of variance in
-staleness scores, versus 76% for the subjective well-being battery alone: an objective marker
-(catecholamines) did add predictive value in the primary study. The book's statement that "use
-of a larger battery of indicators did not increase the accuracy" is not supported by this
-abstract; that specific claim should be read as the book's own retelling, not confirmed against
-the source study.
-**Why it works** — The duration cap follows directly from stacking two decay clocks against
-each other: fatigue from concentrated intense work saturates in 3-4 weeks, and the prior
-mesocycle's basic-ability residual (aerobic endurance, max strength, ~30 days per
-[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]) also runs out around then, so
-a transmutation mesocycle that runs longer risks both overtraining and arriving at competition
-with degraded basic abilities. The book's own retelling of the Hooper et al. (1995) finding
-(that cheap subjective ratings out-predicted an expensive blood/hormone panel) is presented as
-evidence that systematic self-report monitoring is not a "budget substitute" for physiological
-testing in this specific application. Issurin conditions this on the ratings being "used
-systematically and responsibly" (PDF p. 122, printed p. 111) and on "much confidence between
-the coach and athlete" (Table 3.11, PDF p. 120, printed p. 109); the primary-abstract check
-above qualifies, but does not reverse, the book's retelling.
-**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college football calendar** — The **middle-to-late
-weeks of fall camp**, where two-a-days and the highest-intensity, most sport-specific
-(scrimmage-heavy) work concentrate, are functionally a transmutation mesocycle and should be
-capped near the same 3-4 week outer limit Issurin gives, both to avoid overtraining and because
-any aerobic/strength base built in an early-camp or summer accumulation phase will itself decay
-on roughly the same clock. Any old-school "keep hammering all camp" plan without at least one
-built-in restorative window or aerobic mini-block runs against both duration-limiting factors
-here at once. **Eric's baseline** does not name Snell's overtraining definition or the
-five warning signs; see When NOT to apply for how the baseline's own daily-wellness-survey
-history relates to the Hooper et al. finding above.
-**When NOT to apply** — **Inference, population caveat:** every piece of
-supporting evidence in this section (Sharobajko's kayakers referenced upstream, Hooper's
-swimmers, Snell's own middle-distance-running background) comes from individual
-endurance/technical sports, not football; the 3-4 week duration cap is Issurin's own applied
-synthesis with no controlled dose-response citation (the 5 beats/min-over-3-5-days resting-HR
-threshold, by contrast, is credited in the text to Burke et al., 1990, and Hooper et al.,
-1995, not offered as Issurin's own synthesis). **Eric's baseline:** the department's own
-SportSmith-documented history is directly relevant here, not as a contest of this entry's
-rating but as a scope note. Eric's baseline describes a daily wellness survey rolled out via
-the AMS app that was abandoned after about a year because "athletes learned to game" its
-consistent, low-effort answers; it is still used, deliberately, in return-to-play scenarios
-and with athletes managing chronic conditions, where subjective context adds value objective
-data cannot supply (`method-baseline.md`, "Load monitoring and GPS," citing
-`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`). Read against Hooper et al. as retold in the book, this is
-not a validity dispute (both sources treat structured subjective self-report as informative
-when used well); it is a **response-integrity problem at roster scale**. Issurin himself
-conditions the book's claim on ratings being "used systematically and responsibly" (PDF p. 122,
-printed p. 111) and on "much confidence between the coach and athlete" (Table 3.11, PDF p. 120,
-printed p. 109), exactly the condition the baseline's gamed survey failed at scale (a 120+
-player roster over an academic year-plus) that a 14-19-swimmer, 6-month research cohort was not
-tested against. The library agrees with the book's general direction: vault
-`research-papers/thorpe-2017-monitoring-fatigue-status-in-elite-team-sport-athletes-implications-for-practice.md`
-finds self-report responsive to load, and
-`research-papers/mccall-2023-a-qualitative-study-of-11-world-class-team-sport-athletes-experiences-answering-subjective.md`
-frames honest responding as a relational, not purely instrument-design, problem: consistent
-with reading the baseline's experience as a response-integrity failure rather than a rebuttal
-of Hooper's finding. Issurin's own later peer-reviewed review states that block-periodization
-evidence generally "does not supply validated block durations or effect estimates for
-collegiate American football" (Issurin, 2016, *Sports Medicine*, vault
-`research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a.md`).
-**Example** — **Inference:** a mid-fall-camp week showing a player's self-reported fatigue,
-stress, sleep and soreness ratings all climbing together over several days would meet Issurin's
-stated early-warning pattern for overtraining, per the book's retelling of the Hooper et al.
-case, even before any blood marker moved; per the primary abstract, an objective marker
-(resting plasma catecholamines) also contributed to predicting staleness in that same study, so
-this should be read as "subjective ratings are a highly efficient first signal," not "resting
-HR alone caught it and objective markers added nothing."

+ratings, and a multi-component model using those four subjective ratings predicted competitive
+performance changes; adding more objective indicators did not improve prediction accuracy.

+daily self-rating log (fatigue, stress, sleep, soreness), itself a daily wellness check, not
+a separate instrument from what it is being compared against (PDF p. 121, printed p. 110).

+Exercise* 27:106-112, retrieved via Europe PMC):** the study monitored **14** swimmers, not
+19 as the book states. Staleness was classified partly *from* prolonged, high fatigue-rating
+levels, which makes a fatigue-rating prediction of staleness partly circular by construction.
+Late-season stress ratings plus resting plasma catecholamines explained 85% of variance in
+staleness scores, versus 76% for the subjective well-being battery alone: an objective marker
+(catecholamines) did add predictive value in the primary study. The book's statement that "use
+of a larger battery of indicators did not increase the accuracy" is not supported by this
+abstract; that specific claim should be read as the book's own retelling, not confirmed against
+the source study.

+each other: fatigue from concentrated intense work saturates in 3-4 weeks, and the prior
+mesocycle's basic-ability residual (aerobic endurance, max strength, ~30 days per
+[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]) also runs out around then, so
+a transmutation mesocycle that runs longer risks both overtraining and arriving at competition
+with degraded basic abilities. The book's own retelling of the Hooper et al. (1995) finding

+evidence that systematic self-report monitoring is not a "budget substitute" for physiological
+testing in this specific application. Issurin conditions this on the ratings being "used
+systematically and responsibly" (PDF p. 122, printed p. 111) and on "much confidence between

**For this note, no.** It's one document going through write → falsify → revise in order. A second writer would conflict, and the gate depends on the reviewer being separate from the writer. The reviser is running now; after it, one short check and it goes to you.

**In parallel, yes.** Several independent jobs could run alongside it right now, and none of them touch the note:

3. **The reviewers' missing-idea lists,** fed to atomizers as small top-up batches.

The limit is review capacity, not agent count. Every atomized chapter adds a reviewer run and usually a fixer and a round-2 check. Today one chapter took 3-4 agent runs to reach the vault. Running 4-5 books at once is feasible (these agents run in the cloud, so the laptop's memory doesn't matter), but it produces a large batch of reviews landing together.

lines: +type: library-entry
+kind: framework
+domain: strength-and-conditioning
+book: block-periodization--issurin
+chapter: "4.2"
+topic: quadrennial (multi-year) cycle planning
+category: [periodization, multi-year-planning, olympic-cycle]
+confidence: supported
+ingest-tier: full-text
+# The Quadrennial Cycle: Four Generic Year-Directions, Individualized by Stage Objectives
+**What it is** — Issurin frames multi-year planning around the four-year Olympic
+cycle, triggered by post-Games analysis: "the challenge of post-Olympic analysis is to
+internalize positive experiences and reveal the reasons for sub-par performances. Based
+on the findings, a new preparatory plan is worked out" (PDF p. 143, printed p. 132).
+He gives a worked example: the Russian national gymnastics team's quadrennial cycle,
+subdivided into **eight half-year stages**, each with its own general objective (PDF p.
+144, printed p. 133, cited to Arkajev & Suchilin, 2004): (1) enhancement of
+sport-specific motor fitness; (2) acquisition of new, highly complex technical skills and
+their hybrids; (3) updating of competition combinations; (4) further increases in
+sport-specific motor fitness; (5) enhancement of technical mastery and attaining stable
+performances; (6) increase in performance quality, stability and stress tolerance; (7)
+final compilation of competition combinations, endurance for an entire program, and
+selection of a duplicate Olympic squad; (8) modeling expected competitive conditions,
+attaining high competitive reliability, and final selection of the Olympic team. Issurin
+is explicit that this eight-stage division is sport-specific ("a matter of professional
+competence" depending on conditions), and that "the division of the quadrennial cycle
+into four annual cycles is the most popular" in general (PDF p. 144, printed p. 133).
+For the four-annual-cycle version, Table 4.4 (PDF p. 144, printed p. 133; verified
+against the page image) gives generic year-by-year directions, irrespective of sport:
+**Year 1** — engagement and examination of new candidates, selection of coaches and
+staff, updating/correcting training means and methods, remodeling the training
+repertory, forming team spirit and camaraderie; **Year 2** — further candidate selection
+and approval, acquisition of new techno-tactical skills, increased training workloads,
+improved training quality; **Year 3** — attaining maximal training-workload level,
+approving the Olympic-season annual cycle, determining individual performance
+characteristics per team member; **Year 4** — stabilizing team make-up (usually with a
+double Olympic squad), stabilizing workloads at the prior year's level, and approving
+and stabilizing competitive behavior and performance. Issurin states the third and
+fourth years "should be very similar since coaches simulate the annual pre-Olympic
+training design one year before" the Games, though the pre-Olympic (fourth) year's
+workload is "usually higher than the year before for various reasons," including
+"greater motivation, better conditions for training and restoration, greater budgets"
+(PDF p. 146, printed p. 135).
+**Why it works** — The author gives no controlled-comparison mechanism for why
+this generic four-year sequence outperforms an alternative structure; it is presented as
+observed common practice ("the division of the quadrennial cycle into four annual
+cycles is the most popular") rationalized post hoc by the logic of squad-building
+(candidate selection and cohesion before workload escalation, workload escalation
+before stabilization). **Inference:** the underlying logic parallels this library's existing
+long-term athletic development material — building foundational capacity (team
+identity, basic skill acquisition) before layering higher, more specific workloads — but
+Issurin does not state that connection explicitly in this passage.
+**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college context** — College football has no
+literal Olympic quadrennium, but the four-year (or five-year, with a redshirt) eligibility
+window is a structurally similar bounded multi-year cycle with its own roster-cohort
+logic: Year 1 (true freshman/transfer intake) mapping to Table 4.4's Year 1 emphasis on
+candidate evaluation and cultural integration; Years 2-3 to skill/technical acquisition
+and rising training-workload tolerance; a "walk year" (senior or draft-eligible year)
+to Table 4.4's Year 4 emphasis on stabilized, individualized performance. The
+gymnastics eight-stage example is a useful illustration that objective-setting per stage
+should be concrete and sport-specific rather than generic, which is directly usable
+guidance for building a position-group or class-cohort development plan.
+**When NOT to apply** — **Inference, population caveat:** both the eight-stage
+gymnastics example and the four-year Table 4.4 are drawn from Olympic individual/
+team-technical sports with a single fixed quadrennial target and squad continuity
+controlled by national-team selection, not from a college roster with annual signing
+classes, transfer portal turnover, and no shared four-year entry cohort (a program's
+"Year 1" and "Year 4" athletes are present simultaneously every season, unlike a
+national team's cycle-wide cohort). The table's per-year directions are the author's own
+applied synthesis of common practice, not a study with an outcome measure; no
+evidence is given that following this sequence produces better long-term results than
+an alternative one. The Table 4.4 vs Fig. 4.5 age-cohort content (older/experienced vs.
+younger-athlete workload differentiation within this same quadrennial frame) is
+treated separately in
+[[heuristic--older-vs-younger-athlete-quadrennial-workload-differentiation]].
+**Example** — **Inference:** a position group's four-year development plan borrowing
+Table 4.4's shape: Year 1 focused on evaluating and culturally onboarding new signees
+and transfers; Year 2 on techno-tactical (scheme/position) skill acquisition and raising
+training-load tolerance; Year 3 on maximizing training workload and identifying each
+player's individual performance profile; Year 4 on stabilizing role, workload, and
+game-performance consistency for players entering their final season or a likely draft
+evaluation.
+**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/framework--ltad-sequential-model]],
+[[heuristic--older-vs-younger-athlete-quadrennial-workload-differentiation]],
+[[framework--long-term-preparation-four-stage-model-and-directions]].
+type: library-entry
+kind: framework
+domain: strength-and-conditioning
+book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
+chapter: "4.1.2"
+topic: training effect taxonomy
+category: [programming, adaptation, terminology]
+confidence: supported
+ingest-tier: full-text
+# Acute vs. Delayed, and Particular vs. Cumulative: The Book's Taxonomy of Training Effect
+**What it is** — The authors distinguish the acute (immediate) training effect (ATE), the
+body's short-term improvement or deterioration in functional state right after a strength
+means is applied, from the delayed training effect (DTE), the more stable adaptation that
+follows once the volume of training influence is sufficient (cross-referenced forward to
+chapter 6.7.1, not yet ingested in this pass). Whether the immediate reaction is
+deterioration or improvement is said to depend on the exercise's energy cost, which
+determines the rest interval needed before the next exercise: the interval can be lengthened
+if more rest is needed, or optimally shortened to exploit a beneficial "superimposed
+after-effect phenomenon." Separately, the authors distinguish the particular effect (from
+one or more unidirectional means, reflecting the specificity of that means and regime) from
+the cumulative effect (from a complex of multi-directional means), stating explicitly that
+the cumulative effect is not simply the sum of the body's individual functional changes, but
+"a complex of new forms of its motor potential" that still contains the specific
+characteristics of the particular means used. The authors then state five generalizations
+about the training effect of a complex of means: (1) the training effect of any means
+diminishes as the athlete's special physical fitness increases; (2) the means used should
+produce the optimal training effect relative to the athlete's current functional state; (3)
+the after-effect of previous work alters the training effect of subsequent means; (4) the
+training effect of a complex of means depends not only on the sum of the individual stimuli
+but also on their combination, order of succession and intervals of separation; (5) the
+content of special strength training should be a complex of specific stimuli that produces
+the strength fitness required for the given sport, matched to the athlete's level of sports
+mastery. (PDF pp. 215-216, printed pp. 204-205.)
+**Why it works** — No mechanism is given for the ATE/DTE split beyond the energy-cost-driven
+rest-interval logic, and the claim that a cumulative effect is "not simply the sum" of
+individual effects is stated, not derived. Inference: this is consistent with the general
+principle that a training stimulus interacts with the body's current state (fatigue,
+potentiation, prior adaptation) rather than acting as an independent, additive input, the
+same logic that underlies
+[[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]] in the passage immediately
+following this one.
+**When to apply** — Use the ATE/DTE distinction as a planning lens for ordering exercises
+and sessions around desired short-term versus long-term effects: an ATE expected to
+potentiate the next exercise justifies a shorter rest interval, while one expected to deplete
+justifies a longer one. Use the particular/cumulative distinction to judge whether a training
+block's variety is producing an integrated adaptation or just a list of separate,
+unintegrated stimuli, and use the five generalizations as a checklist when building a
+multi-means training complex.
+**When NOT to apply** — This is a conceptual taxonomy, not an operational protocol. The book
+gives no specific rest-interval numbers here and no method for judging in real time whether a
+given ATE is potentiating or depleting; the fuller treatment is deferred to chapter 6.7.1,
+which is pending in this ingest.
+**Example** — Inference: pairing a heavy back squat (a depleting ATE) immediately before
+max-velocity sprint work would likely blunt that day's sprint quality, while placing the same
+squat after the sprint work, or on a separate day, avoids that particular-effect
+interference. This illustrates the framework; the book does not give this specific case.
+**Related** — [[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]],
+[[framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]].
+type: library-entry
+kind: framework
+domain: strength-and-conditioning
+book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
+chapter: "4.1.2"
+topic: training order and combination effects
+category: [programming, periodization, sequencing]
+confidence: supported
+ingest-tier: full-text
+# Training Is Non-Commutative and Non-Associative: Order and Combination Change the Outcome
+**What it is** — The authors borrow two properties from algebra to describe how combinations
+of training means, methods and techniques behave. The Commutative Law (A*B = B*A) and the
+Associative Law (A*(B*C) = (A*B)*C) are stated to generally NOT hold in sports training.
+Training is non-commutative: the order in which exercises or exercise types are performed
+changes the outcome. The book's own examples: a squat-then-clean sequence does not give the
+same result as clean-then-squat; a distance-running session shortly before a weights session
+"will invariably decrease one's strength capabilities." Training is also non-associative:
+using means A followed by a complex of means B and C does not give the same result as a
+complex of A and B followed by C on its own. The book's own example: a muscle-endurance
+regime (A) performed before a complex of plyometrics (B) and Olympic lifting (C) does not
+produce the same result as a complex of muscle endurance and plyometrics (A and B together)
+followed by Olympic lifting (C) alone. The authors note that with hybrid exercises (several
+movements combined into one repetition, cross-referenced to chapter 7.1, not yet ingested in
+this pass), the order of the individual movements likewise has a major effect on execution
+and effectiveness. (PDF pp. 216-217, printed pp. 205-206.)
+**Why it works** — The authors give no physiological mechanism for non-commutativity or
+non-associativity as such. They tie it to the general after-effect phenomenon: every
+exercise leaves after-effects whose nature, duration and magnitude depend on the intensity,
+duration and pattern of loading, and these after-effects can make exercises placed in
+different parts of a workout, on different training days, or even weeks apart, interact
+positively or negatively. Inference: this is consistent with acute neuromuscular, metabolic
+and potentiation carryover from one exercise or session component to the next, which changes
+the stimulus actually delivered by whatever comes after it, though the book does not name a
+specific physiological carrier for the effect.
+**When to apply** — Use this as an argument against judging a training method in isolation
+from the order, context and combination in which it is used. The book explicitly calls
+blanket statements such as "power cleans are useless," "periodisation doesn't work," or
+"circuit training is excellent for general preparation" simplistic and misleading, because
+virtually any method can be rendered ineffective or harmful through an inappropriate
+combination or timing for a given individual and training stage, while a method that looks
+unremarkable in isolation can be effective as part of the right combination and order.

# Atomization brief (shared by every Flint ingest agent)

Read this whole file before writing anything. It holds the rules the Harries review taught (2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes). The review gate will check every rule here.

## Schema

Follow `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\ingest-book\SKILL.md` exactly: `_domain.md`, `_book.md` (map and resume checkpoint, updated after EACH chapter or unit), and entries named `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md` with kind one of principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim. Use the frontmatter keys exactly as the skill gives them. The body has **What it is** / **Why it works** / **When to apply** / **When NOT to apply** (mandatory, non-trivial) / **Example** / **Related**.

Style reference, read before writing: `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library\strength-and-conditioning\fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer\case-study--isometric-sprinter-and-hurdler.md`, plus one principle file in the same folder.

## Voices: label every one

- **The source author's statements are plain text.**
- **Eric's views** (from `docs/method-baseline.md` or his reviews) are prefixed "Eric's baseline:" or "Eric's review:".
- **Your own reasoning, application or synthesis** is prefixed "Inference:".
- **Nothing unlabeled that the author did not say.** The most common failures: a judgment from Eric's review written as if the author said it; a mechanism the author never gave presented as "why it works" (write "The author gives no mechanism. Inference: ..."); an invented example.

## Lessons from the Supertraining Chapter 1 review (2026-09-26: 30 FIX, 1 NO-GO of 41)

- **Keep the source's internal contradictions.** When a book says X on one page and not-X on another, record both with their pages and set `contested`. Never pick one side silently. The NO-GO entry reversed the book's SJ-CMJ strength-deficit rule because the book states it both ways.
- **Name the right voice.** In co-authored books, write "the authors" unless a passage clearly belongs to one author. A passage that names Verkhoshansky in the third person is Siff writing.
- **Keep `proven` rare and scoped.** Scope it to the replicated core (for example, "Hill's force-velocity curve"), never the whole entry, and mark any disputed sentence inside it. Four of eight `proven` ratings were lowered.
- **No mechanism the source does not give.** About a dozen "Why it works" sections supplied physiology the book never states. Label it "Inference:" or leave it out.
- **Do not add "well established" or "modern research shows" without a citation.** Name the paper, or delete the phrase.

## Lessons from the 2026-09-27 review wave (Supertraining Ch2-3, Issurin Ch3, Bondarchuk, Evans, Old Bull)

- **Invented Examples are the most common failure.** 34 of 36 Supertraining Ch2-3a Examples were unlabelled inventions. Use the source's own example where it gives one; otherwise start the Example with "Inference:".
- **"Verified against the page image" means you opened the image.** Four Issurin Ch3 entries claimed it for figures they had misread (Fig 3.7 inverted, a Table 3.7 row swapped). Sparse slides are not "bare diagrams" until you have looked.
- **Name the population and method the source gives.** Bondarchuk's data are 7,000+ native and foreign athletes, questionnaires, r >= 0.349, steroid-free; entries that said "Soviet athletes" were wrong everywhere.
- **Check what a cited paper actually says.** Issurin 2016's critique targets Verkhoshansky's concentrated-unidirectional model, not Issurin's A-T-R; Herzog & Leonard 2000 shows force enhancement, against the book's sentence. When the book misreports a study, record both.
- **No review history in entries.** "Prior version", "corrected from a NO-GO finding" and similar belong in `staging/fixes_*_applied.md`, never in the entry body.
- **Fix logs must match the files.** One fixer log claimed fixes that were not made. Fixers run their own grep checks and paste the output.
- **Section headers use the vault form** `**What it is** —` (with the em dash). Do not add suffixes such as ": mandatory". Em dashes are banned only in titles and body text. Never wrap a `[[wikilink]]` across lines.

## Evidence

- Every number, definition and quote carries a checkable locator: PDF page (and printed page if it differs), or file plus timestamp. Never write "confirmed in PDF" unless you opened that page.
- Never invent a number. Keep ambiguity visible: mark unclear audio or OCR as unclear, and do not harmonize two conflicting numbers from the source; record both with their locators.
- OCR sources (`staging/ocr/*.md`): pages listed as low_confidence in the header must be checked against the page image before any number from them is cited. Use the Read tool on the PDF page, or render it.

## Confidence

- Practitioner courses and lectures: ceiling `supported`.
- Books: `proven` only for established, widely replicated physiology or mechanics. Soviet-era or single-lab empirical findings and training prescriptions: `supported` at most. `untested` for single cases and anecdotes. `contested` where another library source or modern evidence disagrees (say which).

## Dedup and converge

Before each entry, grep `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library` and the staging library (`C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\staging\library`) for the concept. If it is covered, add a new entry only for a genuinely new angle, and link the existing one in Related. List reciprocal-link suggestions in your final report. Never edit files in the vault or another agent's staging folder.

## Baylor context

Read `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\docs\method-baseline.md` (approved). Use it in When to apply, labelled "Eric's baseline:". Department names: Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine, Applied Performance. Plain style, no em dashes. Use commas, colons and parentheses.

## Scope and output

- Write ONLY into your assigned staging folder. No git, no vault edits.

The *CFTS* OCR has **all 11 chapters, in order**, but I can't confirm every page is there. The text is usable with care, and it's in better shape than the Zatsiorsky OCR.

**Completeness:**
- Each table-of-contents title opens its chapter at a sensible place in the scan, from "Talent Identification" (PDF 16) to "Financial Aspects" (PDF 207).
- The 12 blank pages are the blank backs of chapter-divider pages.
- The book has no printed page numbers the OCR can read. So a page missing inside a chapter can't be ruled out from the numbers; it would only show up as a break in the text when reading.

**Text quality:**
- It's single-column Q&A prose, so unlike Zatsiorsky it mostly reads in the right order.
- But there is damage that the "0 low-confidence pages" score missed:
  - An upside-down line reads as gibberish ("pue Sugddpys Suddoq…").
  - Some lines are dropped.
  - Figures such as Fig 6-6 are scrambled labels.
- That's fine for finding content. Quotes, numbers and every figure have to come from the page image.

**Recorded:**
- In `docs/ATOMIZE_BRIEF.md`: the rule that OCR sources are quoted only from page images, with both books as examples.
- In `docs/STATUS.md`: the completeness maps for both books.
- A note that `scripts/ocr_pdf.py` needs better handling of columns and rotated text before the next scanned book.
- Committed and pushed as `cced90f` on `step1-triage`.

**Still running:** the three atomizers (*Supertraining* Ch4, Issurin Ch4-5, Zatsiorsky Ch1-2), the synthesis reviser, and the CVASPS transcription.

I've done 1 and 2 and the peaking synthesis is drafted for your review. The draft went through an independent falsification review and one revision, and I've spot-checked the revision myself.

**1. Background jobs.** They run one after the other now, because running them together is what ran out of memory.

**2. Issurin 2016 brief in the vault.** It now says the model the review criticises is Verkhoshansky's, not Issurin's A-T-R. It also names the real 2008-vs-2016 difference, which is about amateur athletes (`6ba090b`). While I was in there I made two related vault fixes:
- Two Issurin entries quoted a sentence as Issurin's that the brief's writer actually wrote; they're now relabelled Inference (`bd60c47`).
- The in-season entry had the Saturday-game shift wrong: lifts go on Monday-Tuesday, not Sunday-Monday (`6e1ff32`).

**3. Peaking synthesis.** It's at `docs/synthesis/peaking-and-taper-in-season-football.md` on `step1-triage` (`f6a3410`), with the reusable template in `docs/synthesis/_TEMPLATE.md`.
- **The central point:** every peaking model in the library is built for one event (swimmers, kayakers, throwers). Football has 12+ weekly games and no single peak.
- **The review found real errors, now fixed:** a misread of Issurin's week, a recovery window that clashed with the recommended heavy days, a "supported" label on a 48-hour rule no source gives, and your course's residual numbers counted as independent when they're Issurin's table.
- **Length:** 1,921 body words against a ~1,600 target. Further cuts would drop verified caveats.

**Bottom line of the note:**
1. **Every game week:** one heavy lower-body session (load high, fewer sets) and one planned max-velocity exposure. The strength part is supported as a minimum; the speed part is contested, and there are no football data.
2. **Heavy work early, volume down from Thursday.** Issurin and one D-I program disagree on which day carries the heaviest practice. The roughly 48 hours from the last heavy session to kickoff is my inference, untested.
3. **Read readiness from CMJ strategy metrics** (mRSI or FT:CT) against each player's own norm, with thresholds set from their typical error. Supported in direction; the football samples are small.
4. **Keep aerobic and repeat-effort conditioning every week.** Contested: your class-4 slide and Mujika and Padilla 2000 say aerobic fitness is lost fastest; Issurin says the opposite.
5. **A real taper (1-3 weeks, volume down 40-60%, intensity kept)** only before a single peak after a game-free gap, such as a bowl. Untested in football.

**Your answers finish the note:**
1. What does "peak" mean for us: every Saturday, target games, or only the postseason?
2. Where do our heaviest lifts and practices sit? A Saturday-shifted Issurin week lifts at 48-72 hours post-game, while fast force is still down.
3. Is the class-4 "aerobic is lost fastest" slide your view, and are the course's in-season rules yours?
4. How are bye weeks used now, and does that differ by position?
5. Which mRSI drop, on which day, should change the plan, and do linemen and low-snap players get their own thresholds?
6. Does the postseason get its own 1-3 week taper?

- The atomizers: *Supertraining* 4.2 and 4.3, Issurin Ch4-5, and Zatsiorsky Ch1-2.
- The review of the *Supertraining* 4.1 entries.

  - **Two-factor equation misread.** I rendered the formula at 900 dpi. The page prints `P₀ + P₁e^(−k₁t) − P₂e^(−k₂t)`, and the book calls k₁ and k₂ "time constraints" (sic). The entry and `_book.md` both give it as `e^(−t/k)` "time constants" and say it was "recovered from the image".

  - **Four-features wrongly says individualization is "not developed".** Printed p. 10 has a full section on it.
  - **1st-edition cross-check does not hold up.**

    - Supertraining `joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer` cites the same Zatsiorsky & Raitsin 1974 study as the transfer entry.

  5. Specificity rises with mastery: for beginners, almost any exercise transfers.

-# Joint Strength Curves, Sticking Points, and the Moment-Arm Transformation to End-Point Force
-**What it is** — A **strength curve** plots the external force (or moment of force) an
-athlete can exert at a given motion against body posture/joint angle. Fmm is a function of
-muscular force that undergoes two transformations: muscle-tendon force → joint moment
-(torque, M = Fd, where d is the moment arm) → external end-point force (strength). Single-
-joint strength curves take three general shapes: ascending, descending, or concave (figure
-2.21). Worked examples (Zatsiorsky & Raitsin, 1973; n=24): elbow flexion strength peaks
-near 90° (about 100% of Fmm) and falls to roughly 46-50% near full extension/flexion
-(figure 2.22a); shoulder flexion strength is highest with the arm slightly behind the trunk
-(around −30°, ~100%) and falls to about 37% at 150° (figure 2.22b). The weakest position in
-a joint's range is the **sticking point**: the heaviest weight liftable through a full
-range of motion cannot exceed the strength at the sticking point, even though other
-positions in the range are stronger. Muscle length itself changes tension via two factors:
-overlapping actin/myosin cross-bridge availability, and the contribution of elastic
-(mainly parallel elastic) components: as a general rule (with a few exceptions, e.g. the
-rectus femoris in some cyclists) muscles exert smaller tension at smaller lengths and higher
-tension when stretched. Moment arm also changes with joint angle: the text's own example is
-the biceps brachii (long head), whose moment arm was 11.5 mm at 180° (full extension) and
-45.5 mm at 90° (elbow flexion): a fourfold difference: meaning that if muscle tension
-were identical at both angles, the moment of force (and thus external strength) would
-change fourfold purely from the moment-arm change (printed p. 43, figure 2.24). For
-two-joint muscles (e.g. gastrocnemius), Fmm at one joint depends on the angular position of
-the *other* joint the muscle crosses: when the knee is maximally flexed and the ankle
-plantarflexed, the shortened gastrocnemius cannot produce active plantar-flexion force: a
-position usable for selectively training the soleus instead. (PDF pp. 49-54, printed pp.
-**Why it works** — The mechanism is explicitly two-part and stated directly by the authors:
-(1) muscle tension varies with muscle length (cross-bridge overlap plus elastic-component
-contribution), and (2) the moment arm of that muscle force varies with joint angle
-independent of tension itself; strength at any joint angle is their product (figure 2.24: a
-muscle tension-angle curve × a moment-arm-angle curve = the resulting joint torque curve).
-**When to apply** — As a quantified, citable rationale for coaching cues about
-range-specific loading and for anticipating where in a lift's range an athlete will be
-weakest (the sticking point), useful for accommodating-resistance programming (bands,
-chains) or partial-range strength work targeted at a known sticking point. **Eric's
-baseline:** this complements, rather than duplicates,
-[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--torque-optimization-in-lifting-technique]]
-(bar-path/torque-minimization coaching cues) and
-[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--joint-angle-and-limb-position-changes-force-output]]
-(a separate set of joint-angle findings, e.g. forearm pronation, trunk flexion, head tilt,
-from later in Supertraining); this entry supplies the moment-arm mechanism (the
-11.5-to-45.5-mm biceps example, fourfold difference) underlying why those position effects

-peak ~90°, shoulder flexion peak near −30°, the 11.5/45.5 mm biceps figures) are
-single-study data (Zatsiorsky & Raitsin, 1973 and 1992) from a specific population (n=24);
-do not assume they transfer exactly to a different joint, muscle, or population without
-verification. The rectus femoris exception (higher tension at shorter length, in some
-cyclists) is noted as an exception to the general muscle-length rule, not a contradiction of

**Yes, there's a plan, but it doesn't mean reading everything.** Here's where each piece stands:

| Step | What it means | Where it stands |
|---|---|---|
| 0. Catalog | List every Drive file, no AI tokens spent | **Done.** 17,847 files, 11,654 unique |
| 1. Your baseline | Your own method, which every source is compared against | **Done.** Your interview (27 questions) is still pending |
| 2. Triage | Sort every file into A (deep-ingest), B (catalog only) or C (skip), then a ranked shortlist per discipline for you to approve | **Stalled.** Simple rules sorted 59%; 3,998 files are unsorted, and no shortlist exists yet |
| 3. Route tier A | Papers to Zotero, courses and books to the vault behind the review gate, video to transcription | **Only a small, hand-picked slice so far:** Landon's queue and the Harries and Old Bull courses |
| 4. Synthesize | One note per discipline, compared against your method | First note drafted (peaking), waiting on your answers |

**The honest arithmetic:**

| Route | Files |
|---|---:|
| Papers → Zotero | 4,746 |
| Your own reports (archived) | 1,942 |
| Courses and slides to atomize | 1,331 |
| Video and audio to transcribe | 1,179 |
| Templates and data (review) | 944 |
| Catalog only | 829 |
| Books | 602 |

Over two days the gated pipeline put about 270 entries from 7 sources into the vault. At that rate, 602 books and 1,331 course files would take years. So the design is:
- **Papers** go into Zotero in bulk, where search makes them usable without atomizing each one.
- **Only a tier-A shortlist** gets deep-ingested.
- **Synthesis notes** are the actual thought-partner layer.

**The gap is step 2.** Everything since day 1 has come from your hand-picked queue, because the shortlists don't exist yet.

**What I'd start in the new session: finish triage and draft the tier-A shortlists.** It's the step that turns "a lot more content" into a ranked plan, and it doesn't touch the book folders the current agent is working in. Paste this, run from the same worktree folder:

Commit on `step1-triage` and write your own handoff in `docs/handoffs/`. Spin up subagents as needed.

**One thing only you can do,** and it's worth more than either session: answer the six peaking questions and do the 27-question interview (`docs/interview-prep.md`). Every synthesis note is blocked on "where Eric lands", and no amount of ingest fills that in.

The current agent is still running the handoff and will promote whatever passes its checks. I'll report when it finishes.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Gmail__send_message
entries.description:
Sends a new email message immediately from the authenticated user's Gmail account.

To send an existing draft message, provide the `draftId`. To send a new message, provide recipients in `to`, `cc`, or `bcc`, a `subject`, and message content in `body` or `htmlBody` (plain text in `body`, rich HTML in `htmlBody`; do NOT format `body` with Markdown). To thread the message under an existing thread or conversation, provide `replyThreadId` (preferred for send-only clients) or `replyToMessageId`. If sending a new message, attachments can be included via the `attachments` field, but the combined size cannot exceed 25MB.

Returns a Message object with the `id`, `threadId`, and `labelIds` fields populated.

attachments.description: Optional. The attachments to include in the email. The combined size of attachments in the message cannot exceed 25MB. If you need to send files larger than 25MB, upload the file to Drive first and then insert the Drive link into `body` or `html_body`.

bcc.description: Optional. The blind carbon copy recipients of the email. Each string MUST be a valid plain email address (e.g., "user@example.com").

body.description: Optional. The plain text body content of the email. Do NOT format this field with Markdown (such as headers `#`, bold `**`, bullet points `*`, or tables `|`). If formatted rich text is desired, use `html_body` instead. If `html_body` is also provided, this field is treated as the plain-text alternative.

cc.description: Optional. The carbon copy recipients of the email. Each string MUST be a valid plain email address (e.g., "user@example.com").

draftId.description: Optional. The unique identifier of an existing draft to send. If provided, the other fields (`to`, `cc`, `bcc`, `subject`, `body`, `html_body`) are ignored, and the specified draft is sent as is.

htmlBody.description: Optional. The HTML content of the email. If provided, this will be used as the rich-text version of the email. Use this field (with valid HTML tags such as ` `, `

replyThreadId.description: Optional. The unique identifier of the thread to send this message in. If provided, the sent message will be threaded under the specified thread. Compatible with all scopes including send-only (gmail.send).

replyToMessageId.description: Optional. The unique identifier of the message to reply to. If provided, this message will be threaded in reply to the specified message. Note: Resolving a message by ID requires read permissions (e.g., 'gmail.modify' or 'gmail.compose'). If the caller only has send-only permissions ('gmail.send'), use `reply_thread_id` instead.

subject.description: Optional. The subject line of the email.

to.description: Optional. The primary recipients of the email. Required if `draft_id` is not provided. Each string MUST be a valid plain email address (e.g., "user@example.com").

Attachment.description: Represents an attachment to be included in an email.

content.description: Required. The base64-encoded content of the attachment.

filename.description: Optional. The name of the file to be attached, e.g. "invoice.pdf". For inline attachments, this is used for Content-ID generation. For regular attachments, `filename` is used to specify the filename to email clients. If not provided, the attachment may be received with no name.

id.description: Optional. Output only. When present, contains the ID of an external attachment that can be retrieved in a separate `GetMessageAttachment` request.

inline.description: Optional. If true, this attachment is handled as inline. An inline attachment is a content that is intended to be displayed within the body of an HTML email, as opposed to being listed as a separate file for download. If false or absent, defaults to false, and it's treated as a regular attachment.

mimeType.description: Optional. The field representing a content or media type must use IANA MIME type, https://www.iana.org/assignments/media-types/media-types.xhtml. If not provided, defaults to "application/octet-stream".

Reminder for tomorrow, Monday 9/28: the Flint interview session. It is the one step only you can do, and every synthesis note is waiting on it.

The attached flint-interview.ics adds an all-day event to your calendar. Move it to whatever time suits you.

How to start:
1. In PowerShell: cd C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage
2. Run: claude
3. Say: "Run /interview-me using docs/interview-prep.md, then walk me through the six questions in docs/synthesis/peaking-and-taper-in-season-football.md, section 8."

What it covers:
- Interview prep: 27 questions about your method (docs/interview-prep.md). They turn it into written decision rules: "when X, I do Y, because Z".
- Peaking synthesis: 6 questions that finish the first synthesis note:
  1. In a 12-plus game season, what does "peak" mean for us: every Saturday, target games, or only the postseason?
  2. Where do our heaviest lifts and practices sit in a game week? Should heavy and high-velocity work wait until Wednesday, given that fast force is still down 48 to 72 hours after a game?
  3. Is the class-4 slide's "aerobic is lost fastest" your view, and are the course's in-season rules yours?
  4. How are bye weeks used now, and does that differ by position?
  5. Which mRSI drop, on which day, changes the plan? Do linemen and low-snap players get their own thresholds?
  6. Does the postseason get its own 1 to 3 week taper?

Status: today's Flint work is committed on branch step1-triage. Two background agents were still running when this was sent: one finishing the book ingest and promotion, one triaging the rest of the Drive.

(Sent by Claude Code from the Flint session.)

The reminder is sent to both eric.rash11@gmail.com and eric_rash@baylor.edu, as one email with no separate forward.
- **The email** has the steps to start tomorrow's session, the six peaking questions, and a pointer to the 27 interview questions.
- **The attachment** is `flint-interview.ics`: an all-day event on Monday 9/28 with a reminder the evening before. Open it in Outlook to add it to your calendar, then move it to whatever time suits you. I can't write to your Outlook calendar directly.

**Two agents are running in the background:**
- **The handoff agent:** finishing the *Supertraining*, Issurin and Zatsiorsky batches, then promoting whatever passes into the vault under your pre-approval.
- **The triage agent:** classifying the ~4,000 unsorted Drive files and drafting per-discipline tier-A shortlists in `docs/shortlists/`. It won't touch the other agent's files.

I'll report each result when it comes back. Keep this session open until both finish.

-# Residual Training Effects Last Different Numbers of Days for Different Motor Abilities
-**What it is** — The residual training effect is defined as "the retention of changes
-induced by systematic workloads beyond a certain time period after the cessation of
-training," a term Issurin attributes to Brian and James Counsilman (1991) (PDF p. 33,
-printed p. 22). Issurin & Lustig (2004) is cited as the source of Table 1.6 (PDF p. 35,
-printed p. 24), giving residual duration ± SD in days after cessation of training for each
-motor ability: **aerobic endurance 30 ± 5 days**, **maximum strength 30 ± 5 days**,
-**anaerobic glycolytic endurance 18 ± 4 days**, **strength endurance 15 ± 5 days**,
-**maximum speed (alactic) 5 ± 3 days**. Table 1.6's own physiological-background column
-lists aerobic endurance's residual as resting on increased aerobic enzymes, mitochondria,
-muscle capillaries, hemoglobin capacity, glycogen storage, and fat-metabolism rate, and
-maximum strength's on improved neural mechanism and muscle hypertrophy from fiber
-enlargement, with no percentages attached in the table itself. Later in the text (PDF p. 35,
-printed p. 24), Issurin gives a specific figure for one of those table items: aerobic
-enzymes increase by 40-90% with training (Volkov, 1986; Fox et al., 1993; Wilmore & Costill,
-1993). He contrasts this with much smaller local adaptations from sprint training:
-phosphocreatine storage (+2-5%), peak lactate accumulation (+10-20%), and anaerobic enzymes
-(+2-20%), given without a citation on that page. On the following page (PDF p. 36, printed
-p. 25), Thorstensson (1988) is cited specifically for "relatively small increases" in
-quickly available energy sources, ATP and phosphocreatine, and enzymes such as creatine
-kinase, from highly concentrated sprint training.
-**Why it works** — Issurin states the mechanism directly (PDF pp. 35-36, printed pp. 24-25):
-aerobic ability, supported by pronounced morphological and biochemical changes, is retained
-"for a number of weeks at near-peak level," while anaerobic abilities, particularly maximum
-sprint speed, "retain near-peak levels for much shorter periods" because peak speed's gains
-are smaller and rest on "very delicate and highly precise neuro-muscular interactions, which
-are relatively unstable and cannot be maintained at the highest level without specially
-organized training." Maximum strength's comparably long residual is attributed to pronounced
-morphological, biochemical, and neural changes: enlargement of muscle-fiber cross-sectional
-area, hyperplasia, recruitment of previously inactive motor units, synchronization of their
-activity, and increased motor-neuron discharge frequency (Zatsiorsky, 1995). Strength
-endurance's residual is stated to depend on event duration and the degree of
-anaerobic-resource mobilization; longer-duration strength endurance has a relatively longer
-residual thanks to aerobic adaptation.
-**When to apply** — Sequencing which ability to develop first in a training stage (see
-[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]). **Inference:** an ability
-with a long residual (aerobic endurance, max strength, 30 ± 5 d) can be built early and
-carried further without direct work than a short-residual one, but a stage longer than about
-30 days after accumulation ends needs a retention dose (see Example); max speed (5 ± 3 d)
-needs re-exposure close to competition. **Eric's baseline directly echoes half of this table:** "Training
-residual effects set the retraining cadence: aerobic capacity and max strength both need
-re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days or tissue
-readiness for max-velocity work degrades" (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and
-programming," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` p.27). This 30/30/5-day
-pattern matches Issurin's 30±5 / 30±5 / 5±3 figures because it is this table:
-week1-lecture.md (marker p.66) reproduces Table 1.6 directly, under a slide block that names
-"Issurin (Block Training Text)" as a source (marker p.64), and gives strength endurance as
-~12 days against Issurin's 15±5, the one value where the course departs from the book.
-**When NOT to apply** — Treat the numbers as a synthesized rule of thumb
-(±5, ±4, ±5, ±3 day spreads are themselves wide relative to the means), not a precise
-per-athlete clock; Issurin does not report the sample or method behind Issurin & Lustig
-(2004) in this text, so the table's evidentiary base cannot be checked further from this
-source alone. Issurin's own surrounding text also notes limits on how far residual-effect
-thinking travels: maximum oxygen uptake in highly trained endurance athletes falls when
-weekly training volume drops below a certain level (Steinacker, 1993; Steinacker et al.,
-1998), and large volumes of highly intense exercise do not prevent detraining and loss of
-aerobic endurance during a taper (Mujika, 1999) (PDF p. 34, printed p. 23).
-**Contested, flag this directly to Eric:** a *different* part of the same baseline corpus
-states the opposite ordering for detraining rate: "the traits easiest to build (aerobic) are
-lost fastest under detraining; the traits hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest"
-(`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md` p.47).
-This conflicts with Table 1.6 (aerobic residual is the *longest*, tied with strength, at
-30±5 days, while alactic speed is the *shortest* at 5±3 days). The class-1 transcript is
-not a third, independent data point against class-4-2026.md: it also states that aerobic
-capacity is gained and lost very quickly (marker pp.25, 28), gives its 30-day retention
-windows as conditional on "a small retention load" continuing during that window (marker
-p.28), a different construct from Issurin's residual *after cessation* of training, and
-ties its 5-day speed figure to connective-tissue and nervous-system readiness ("otherwise
-the nervous system doesn't change a whole lot," marker p.28) rather than to speed itself
-decaying in 5 days. The course's own numbers come directly from this table (week1-lecture.md
-marker pp.64, 66, strength endurance given there as ~12 days against Issurin's 15±5). Resolve
-with Eric: this may be residual effect after cessation (Issurin, Table 1.6) versus rate of
-loss without any retention dose (class-4-2026.md), two different constructs the corpus does
-not itself reconcile. Do not harmonize these; record all three with their locators and keep
-`contested`, with this as the stated reason.
-**Inference:** this table also converges with, but is not identical to, the vault's
-Verkhoshansky-staging entry on heterochronic adaptation
-([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]],
-staging), which describes a *different* mechanism (order of biochemical sub-processes
-gained/lost) rather than absolute day-counts per motor ability; both describe
-heterochronicity in de-training, but at different levels of description; do not treat them
-as restating the same specific claim.
-**Example** — **Inference:** in a training stage that opens with 4 weeks of accumulation
-(building aerobic base and max strength) followed by 3 weeks of transmutation and 2 weeks of
-realization, competition falls 35 days after accumulation ends: at the outer edge of the
-aerobic and strength residuals' 30 ± 5-day window, not safely inside it. A coach relying on
-this table would want a maintenance dose of both qualities somewhere in transmutation, not
-an assumption that accumulation-phase gains are still fully in hand. Maximum speed work
-needs re-introduction within about 5 days of the target competition, or its residual will
-have decayed well below peak by competition day.
-**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
-[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]] (a ratio-based rule for
-fatigue-vs-fitness decay, distinct from this table's absolute per-ability day counts:
-cross-reference, do not conflate),
-[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]] (staging),
-[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]] (staging).

-# Evans's Own Caveat: the Fitness-Fatigue Model Is "Just a Concept," Not an Empirically Validated Model
-**What it is** — Evans's slide (U1 L5 p.3-4) introduces the Fitness-Fatigue Model ("Fatigue
-can mask fitness") and then immediately qualifies it: "Theoretical Model, only useful if you
-provide evidence. Marathon running... 400m runner? Strength, speed, jumping, aerobic
-capacity, etc... No empirical evidence to put a model together with all the biomotor
-qualities together. JUST A CONCEPT" (capitalization as on the slide). He does not cite a
-specific paper making this critique; it reads as his own assessment, offered in his own
-lecturing voice.
-**Why it works** — This is Evans's own critical framing, not a claim he attributes to another
-author; he does not explain in this slide what evidentiary standard would satisfy him (what a
-validated fitness-fatigue model would need to show), only that one is currently missing for
-combining multiple biomotor qualities into a single model. Inference: his examples (a
-marathon runner needing one kind of fitness-fatigue tradeoff, a 400m runner needing several
-combined - "Strength, speed, jumping, aerobic capacity") suggest his specific objection is
-that the model has not been validated for combining heterogeneous biomotor qualities into one
-curve, as opposed to a single-quality version of the model.
-**When to apply** — As a caution against treating fitness-fatigue modeling (or any
-readiness-curve model built on it) as a validated predictive tool for multi-quality sports
-like American football, where an athlete's readiness depends on strength, speed, and aerobic
-capacity simultaneously. Eric's baseline: this is directly relevant to its own distinction
-between "preparedness" and "readiness" (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment"),
-which uses fitness-fatigue-adjacent language without citing a specific validated model
-either. Inference: Evans's caveat suggests that gap in Eric's baseline material is not unique
-to Baylor's documentation, but reflects a broader unresolved state of the underlying theory.
-The library's Supertraining book (`supertraining--verkhoshansky`) stages its own
-fitness-fatigue framework entry (`framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing.md`);
-a reviewer comparing the two should note that Evans's course explicitly flags the model as
-under-validated in the same breath as teaching it, which the Supertraining entry (not
-reviewed for this comparison) may or may not do.
-**When NOT to apply** — Evans's own caveat is itself unsupported by a named
-citation ("no empirical evidence" is asserted, not referenced to a specific review or
-meta-analysis), so it should be read as his professional judgment, not a sourced literature
-claim. Do not use this entry as evidence that the fitness-fatigue model is definitively
-unsupported in the broader literature; it records only that Evans, in this lecture, said it
-lacks empirical evidence for multi-quality application. Confidence is untested.
-**Example** — Inference: the slide contrasts "Marathon running" with a 400m runner's many
-qualities ("Strength, speed, jumping, aerobic capacity"); the single-quality reading of the
-marathon example (largely one biomotor quality, aerobic endurance) is the writer's, not
-stated on the slide, which may equally mean marathon running is where evidence exists.
-**Related** — Reciprocal-link suggestion:
-`supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing.md` (same
-underlying model, different source, worth cross-referencing this critique against whatever
-mechanism that entry gives). `periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio.md`
-(vault entry on the same fitness-fatigue model from a different named source, worth
-cross-referencing).

-# The Classic Hyperbolic Force-Velocity Curve Breaks Down Near Isometric, and Has Several Modeling Limits
-**What it is** — Hill's classical force-velocity equation, (F+a)(V+b) = (Fo+a)b (a
-hyperbola), was derived largely from isolated (in vitro) muscle. Perrine and Edgerton
-(1978), using in vivo human measurement, found the curve is **not simply hyperbolic near
-zero velocity**: instead of rising smoothly to an asymptote as velocity approaches zero,
-force/torque takes a more parabolic shape and actually peaks at a certain *low* (non-zero)
-velocity before dropping to a lower value under true isometric conditions (V=0): that is,
-maximum torque is not produced isometrically. Above roughly 200 degrees/second, Hill's
-hyperbolic relation still holds. Separately, Herzog (1996) lists concrete limitations of
-using force-length and force-velocity relationships to predict individual muscle force in
-practice: the force-length relation is unknown for most human muscles, is plastic/adaptable
-under elite training demands, differs between maximal and submaximal contraction, differs
-with which length is held constant experimentally, and differs between electrically-stimulated
-and voluntary contraction; the force-velocity relation is similarly unknown for individual
-muscles, differs sharply between maximal and submaximal activation, differs between
-force-controlled and velocity-controlled conditions, and inadequately accounts for
-stretch-related (SSC) processes: stretch-shortening/plyometric force-velocity behavior
-does not follow the standard inverse hyperbolic pattern at all (cf. Bosco 1982's finding
-that plyometric training lets muscle produce more force after depth-jump training). Isometric
-force itself also depends on contraction *history* (higher after a stretch than under pure
-isometric hold, lower after a tension release), which is not captured in standard
-force-velocity models. (PDF pp. 158-159, printed pp. 147-148, "3.3.2 The Effect of the Load
-on Speed of Muscle Contraction," "Limitations of the Force-Velocity Relation," Fig 3.15.)
-**Why it works** — No single mechanism is offered for the Perrine-Edgerton deviation; the
-text simply reports it as an empirical in vivo finding that conflicts with Hill's in vitro
-model. **Inference:** possible contributors include the parallel elastic and series elastic
-tissue contributions present in an intact human joint but not in isolated muscle
-preparations, and the difficulty (noted by Herzog) of measuring true sarcomere-level length
-and force in vivo, since sarcomeres do not behave linearly relative to whole muscle-tendon
-length (Zajac & Gordon, 1989).
-**When to apply** — Use this as a caution against treating the textbook hyperbolic
-force-velocity curve as a precise predictive model for an individual athlete's real,
-in vivo force output, especially near isometric/very-low-velocity conditions or for
-stretch-shortening-cycle actions. It directly qualifies [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]]
-(Ch1): the general specificity logic of that principle still holds, but the exact shape of
-the curve near V=0 and under SSC conditions is more complex than the simple hyperbola implies.
-**When NOT to apply** — Contested within the book: Hill's hyperbola (printed 146) vs
-Perrine and Edgerton's in vivo curve, which peaks at a low non-zero velocity (printed 148);
-the book does not reconcile them. Perrine-Edgerton's in vivo curve is one dataset (1978),
-not a full replacement validated across muscle groups and populations. The book itself does
-not offer a neural or other mechanism for why the two curves diverge. Do not use this to discard force-velocity profiling
-broadly: it is a caution about precision near the isometric end and under SSC conditions
-specifically, not a rejection of the underlying force-velocity trade-off. Separately, the
-book states plainly that "the Hill and Perrine-Edgerton curves do not apply to actions
-which strongly recruit the stretch reflex or involve the release of stored elastic energy"
-(printed 152), which further narrows where either curve should be trusted.
-**Example** — **Inference:** a force-velocity profile built from isokinetic dynamometer
-data near zero velocity should not be assumed to predict an athlete's true near-isometric
-force output accurately, per the Perrine-Edgerton finding that peak torque actually occurs
-at a low, non-zero velocity rather than at V=0. This example is not in the source.
-**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (Ch1, the
-general principle this claim adds nuance and caveats to); [[claim--three-zone-force-velocity-curve-for-cyclic-locomotion]]
-(a further, cyclic-specific deviation from Hill's model within this same Ch3 section).
